The Mornington Peninsula's best-known experiences (Peninsula Hot Springs, Arthurs Seat Eagle, Ashcombe Maze, the hatted restaurants) all cost money. There are also genuinely good free options, and several of them are among the strongest things the Peninsula offers.

---

## Completely free

### Coolart Wetlands & Homestead, Somers
One of the quietly rewarding free stops on the Peninsula. A heritage homestead dating to the 1890s, set within extensive wetlands and birdwatching grounds on the Westernport side at Somers. Wheelchair accessible; wheelchairs available to borrow from the Visitor Centre.

**Entry:** Free. **Hours:** Daily 9am–5pm, gates close 5pm sharp. Closed Christmas Day. No booking required.

Lord Somers Road, Somers. [coolart.org.au](https://coolart.org.au)

### Point Nepean National Park, Portsea
The western tip of the Peninsula costs nothing to enter. Vehicle and pedestrian entry is free. Inside the park: over 50 heritage-listed buildings including Fort Nepean, a working quarantine station history, bay swimming at the Quarantine Station beach, and views out across the Heads.

Fort Nepean is approximately 3km on foot from Gunner's Cottage carpark. If you prefer not to walk, the hop-on hop-off internal shuttle runs approximately $12 adult return. Two all-terrain beach wheelchairs and one standard wheelchair are available free from the Information Centre.

**Entry:** Free. Vehicles: 8am–6pm (8am–8pm daylight saving). Pedestrians: any time.

→ [Point Nepean National Park guide](/journal/point-nepean-national-park-guide/)

### Cape Schanck Lighthouse Grounds, Cape Schanck
The 1859 limestone lighthouse and its surrounding grounds are free to access from 6am (verify current hours with Parks Victoria). The boardwalk to Pulpit Rock and the basalt clifftop views are among the strongest on the Peninsula and cost nothing. Lighthouse tours are ticketed (~$16–17 adult on weekends and school holidays), but the walk and views don't require a tour.

<AlertBlock type="warning" heading="Boardwalk works in progress">
Parks Victoria is completing upgrades to the Cape Schanck visitor precinct. Track resurfacing, lookout improvements, and boardwalk works may affect some sections. Follow on-site signage. Works expected complete late April 2026; verify before visiting.
</AlertBlock>

→ [Cape Schanck guide](/journal/cape-schanck-guide/)

### National Park ocean beaches, by foot
All ocean beaches within the Mornington Peninsula National Park are free to access on foot: Sorrento Back Beach, Portsea Back Beach, Gunnamatta, Rye Ocean Beach. Note that dogs are not permitted anywhere in the National Park.

**Important:** PAPP fox baiting and trapping is active from Portsea Ocean Beach to Greens Bush until October 2026. Do not take dogs to any National Park area.

### Foreshore walks, bay beaches
The foreshore paths along the Port Phillip Bay side of the Peninsula are free: Sorrento to Blairgowrie, Rye to Rosebud, the Mornington harbour walk. None of these require paid entry.

---

## Low cost (under $20)

### Pt. Leo Estate Sculpture Park, Merricks ($15 adult, children under 12 free)
330 acres of manicured gardens with permanent works by Yayoi Kusama and KAWS and rotating international exhibitions. One of the more serious sculpture parks in Australia, on a working vineyard. The entry fee is $15 adult; children under 12 are free.

Daily 11am–5pm, last entry 4:30pm. 3649 Frankston-Flinders Road, Merricks.

### Mornington Peninsula Regional Gallery, Mornington (free)
The regional gallery at Mornington runs changing exhibitions and a permanent collection with no entry charge. Hours vary by exhibition; check before visiting.

### Bushrangers Bay Walk, Cape Schanck (free)
The 5.4km return walk from the Cape Schanck eastern carpark to Bushrangers Bay is free. Ocean views, basalt coastline, coastal heathland. Allow approximately two hours return. Note: dogs not permitted (MPNP). Check Parks Victoria for current access; possible secondary closures due to fox control activity.

---

## Seasonal free events

**Mornington Peninsula Pinot Noir Celebration**: typically March; ticketed tastings but free supporting events. Check event calendar.

**Red Hill Market**: first Saturday of the month (except January), Red Hill Showgrounds. Entry free; produce, art, craft stalls.

**Farmers markets**: Mornington, Red Hill, Dromana, and Flinders all run regular farmers markets. Check local schedules for exact dates and entry costs.

---

## A free day itinerary

Start early at Coolart Wetlands (free; 9am opening) for an hour of birdwatching. Drive south to Cape Schanck, park in the lighthouse carpark (free) and walk the boardwalk to Pulpit Rock. Pack lunch and eat on the headland. Afternoon: drive to Portsea and enter Point Nepean National Park (free); walk to Fort Nepean or take the shuttle. Sunset drive back along Point Nepean Road. Total cost: $0 (or ~$24 adult if you take the shuttle and do the lighthouse tour).

Frogspond: A Peninsula producer to verify before you build the day around it

Frogspond vineyard and cellar-door setting on the Mornington Peninsula
Mornington, Mornington Peninsula — roughly 75 to 90 minutes from Melbourne depending on traffic.

Public information on Frogspond is thinner than it is for the Peninsula\'s headline estates, and that usually tells you something useful straight away. It is likely a smaller-scale producer, a private tasting setup, or a venue whose best use is for readers who already know why they are going.

Some of the Peninsula\'s most interesting wine experiences sit behind modest websites, irregular opening hours, and a phone-first booking culture. It does change the approach, though. Frogspond is not the kind of place to send a first-time visitor without a little homework first.

## Why it may still be worth your time

The reason to keep venues like this on the list is simple: the Peninsula works best when it is not reduced to the same handful of big estates. Smaller operators often give you the part that matters most: a clearer sense of who made the wine, what scale they work at, and whether the visit is actually about the bottle rather than the backdrop.

If Frogspond is open for tastings when you want to go, expect a visit that is tighter, quieter, and more specific than the region's major hospitality estates. That is usually a good sign.

### How to approach the visit

Treat Frogspond as a call-ahead address. Worth confirming current access, tasting format, and whether the venue is set up for walk-ins before building a day around it. If the answer is yes, slot it in as one of two stops, not five, and keep lunch elsewhere. That structure gives smaller producers room to be what they are good at.

## How it fits

For readers who like discovering low-profile Peninsula producers, Frogspond is worth keeping on the working list. For first-timers chasing the cleanest possible day out, it works better as a second-trip address after the regional benchmarks are covered.

### What to confirm before you drive

Check whether tastings are by appointment, whether wine sales are direct-to-door only, and whether the venue is operating as a true public cellar door at the moment. Small Peninsula wineries change rhythm seasonally and not all of them update that rhythm clearly online.

The Hatted Restaurants of the Mornington Peninsula

Four two-hat venues, seven one-hat tables, and a debut two-hat restaurant that opened in February. The complete Good Food Guide hat list for the Peninsula, with booking realities and what each restaurant actually is.
Warm, polished restaurant interior with a marble bar, timber stools, and low lighting — the kind of room that suits a Peninsula hatted-restaurant shortlist
Where to Eat on the Mornington Peninsula
Waterfront Restaurants on the Mornington Peninsula
How many hatted restaurants are on the Mornington Peninsula?

The Good Food Guide awarded 15 hats across 11 Peninsula venues, including 4 two-hat restaurants and 7 one-hat restaurants. The Australian Good Food Guide (AGFG) recognises additional venues not in the GFG top list, including Lancemore Lindenderry (AGFG 2 hats) and Paringa Estate (AGFG 1 hat).
What is the best restaurant on the Mornington Peninsula?

By formal recognition, Barragunda Dining (Cape Schanck), Laura (Merricks), Tedesca Osteria (Red Hill), and Ten Minutes by Tractor (Main Ridge) all hold two hats in the Good Food Guide. Tedesca Osteria won Regional Restaurant of the Year. Barragunda is the most recent addition — opened in February, winning two hats in its debut year with the GFG Trailblazer Award.
How far in advance do you need to book at Peninsula hatted restaurants?

Laura at Pt. Leo Estate: book 4 months in advance. Barragunda Dining: essential, very hard to get — book immediately on release. Tedesca Osteria: online booking system only; books out weeks ahead for Friday–Monday lunch sittings. Ten Minutes by Tractor: book 4–8 weeks ahead for lunch, further for dinner. Doot Doot Doot: book 2–4 weeks ahead.
Are there hatted restaurants on the Mornington Peninsula that accept walk-ins?

Rare Hare (Jackalope Hotel, Merricks North) is walk-in only — no reservations taken. Many Little Bar & Dining (Red Hill South) takes walk-ins for evening sessions. Montalto's Piazza is walk-in daily for a more casual experience, even though the main restaurant requires bookings. These are the only hatted-adjacent venues that don't require advance booking.

The Good Food Guide awarded 15 hats to Peninsula restaurants across 11 venues. The Peninsula's hatted scene has changed significantly: Barragunda Dining debuted at two hats in February, Ten Minutes by Tractor has a new head chef (Craig Lunn, ex-Michelin UK), and Tedesca Osteria won Regional Restaurant of the Year. What follows is the accurate hat count, what each restaurant actually is, and the booking reality at each.

## The two-hat restaurants in detail

### Barragunda Dining: Cape Schanck
The newest and most talked-about Peninsula restaurant. Opened in February in a converted 40-seat farmhouse on the 1000-acre Barragunda Estate. Chef Simone Watts (ex-Coda, Pearl Melbourne) won the GFG Trailblazer Award alongside the two-hat debut. The degustation is $145pp and the focus is on estate-grown organic vegetables, hibachi-charred proteins, and exceptional produce sourcing.

Barragunda is operating at the standard that regional Australian restaurants rarely achieve on debut. Urban List ranked it #3 in their Best Melbourne Restaurants list.

**Booking reality:** Essential. Very hard to get. Book immediately when you check availability. Open Friday to Monday, lunch sessions.

113 Cape Schanck Road, Cape Schanck. [barragunda.com.au](https://www.barragunda.com.au)

### Laura: Merricks (Pt. Leo Estate)
Two hats for seven consecutive years. Laura at Pt. Leo Estate sits within the sculpture park and has a Relais & Châteaux membership: the Peninsula's most internationally credentialled restaurant. Josep Espuga is now Culinary Director, succeeding Phil Wood. The menu runs to eight-course chef's journeys and four-course signature formats. Southern Rock lobster with white asparagus and wagyu with yuzu apple are anchor dishes.

The setting: floor-to-ceiling glass overlooking the sculpture lawns and Western Port Bay: and the calibre of the kitchen make this the clearest destination-restaurant case on the Peninsula.

**Booking reality:** Book four months in advance. Thursday to Monday lunch from 12pm; Saturday dinner from 6pm (Friday dinner in peak season).

3649 Frankston-Flinders Road, Merricks. [ptleoestate.com.au](https://www.ptleoestate.com.au/dine/laura/)

### Tedesca Osteria: Red Hill
Regional Restaurant of the Year. Brigitte Hafner's agriturismo restaurant in a converted 1940s house on a biodynamic farm in Red Hill is the most personal restaurant on the Peninsula: chickens, beehives, and Wiltshire Horn sheep supply the kitchen alongside the on-site garden. The format is a five-course set menu with hand-rolled pasta, seafood, and meat, cooked on an open wood-fired grill.

Thirty seats. Lunch only, Friday to Monday. There is no other format and no walk-in option. Accommodation at Graceburn House is attached to the property.

**Booking reality:** Online booking system only. Books out weeks ahead. Book as soon as your date is set.

1175 Mornington-Flinders Road, Red Hill. [tedesca.com.au](https://www.tedesca.com.au)

### Ten Minutes by Tractor: Main Ridge
The Peninsula's most established fine-dining destination. Craig Lunn (appointed late in the year, ex-Michelin kitchens in UK and Europe) now leads the kitchen of Australia's first certified organic Peninsula vineyard restaurant. Two menu formats: the Essence Menu ($145pp) and the Signature Menu ($290pp with wine pairing). An Allis wine bar on-site offers a less formal option Friday to Sunday.

**Booking reality:** Book four to eight weeks ahead for weekend lunch. Book further ahead for dinner. Wednesday to Sunday lunch, Friday and Saturday dinner.

1333 Mornington-Flinders Road, Main Ridge. [tenminutesbytractor.com.au](https://www.tenminutesbytractor.com.au)

---

## The one-hat restaurants in detail

### Doot Doot Doot: Merricks North (Jackalope Hotel)
One hat. Guy Stanaway's dining room at Jackalope Hotel is dinner-only and built around the 10,000-globe chandelier that defines the space. A5 Wagyu MB12, Skull Island tiger prawn, appellation oysters. Eighty seats; open to non-hotel guests. The most interior-design-forward fine dining room on the Peninsula.

**Booking reality:** Book two to four weeks ahead. Dinner nightly from 6pm.

### Rare Hare: Merricks North (Jackalope Hotel)
One hat. Walk-in only: no reservations taken. The informal outdoor dining counterpart to Doot Doot Doot, built around a wood-fired oven. Classic Hare Share feast is $85pp. Dog-friendly on the outdoor lawn. Walk-ins Monday to Friday from 5pm; Saturday and Sunday from 2pm.

### Moke Dining: Flinders
One hat. Michael Cole's family-owned restaurant in Flinders village. Dinner Thursday to Sunday; lunch Saturday and Sunday. Intimate fine dining in a village setting.

### Montalto: Red Hill South
One hat. Three to four-course set menu from $130pp. The Piazza (walk-in daily 11am–5pm) provides a casual alternative. Lunch Friday to Monday in the main restaurant; 1km sculpture trail on the property.

### Polperro Restaurant: Red Hill
One hat. Chef's tasting menu; tea-smoked Aylesbury duck breast. Ancient Angophora trees over the vineyard. Wednesday to Sunday. Sister venue to Many Little Bar & Dining.

### Port Phillip Estate: Red Hill South
One hat. Hatted dining in a striking rammed-earth building with panoramic vineyard-to-bay views. Six accommodation suites on-site. Flinders mussels, farm-fresh lamb. Lunch daily; Friday and Saturday dinner.

### Many Little Bar & Dining: Red Hill South
One hat. Sri Lankan-inspired cooking in a low-key Red Hill South setting. Dog-friendly outdoor seating. Thursday to Sunday from 4pm; Saturday and Sunday from 12pm.

---

## AGFG-recognised restaurants

**Lancemore Lindenderry Dining Room** (Red Hill) holds two AGFG hats and the Readers' Choice Award for several consecutive years. Nick McGonigal leads the kitchen. Dinner Thursday to Saturday, lunch Friday to Sunday. This is a strong destination in its own right despite not appearing in the GFG top 11.

**Paringa Estate** (Red Hill South) holds one AGFG hat. Lunch Wednesday to Sunday, Saturday dinner. The Garden Dining format (shared plates, walk-in Wednesday to Sunday 12–3pm) provides a more casual entry point.

---

## How to approach a hatted Peninsula day

The Peninsula's hatted restaurants are concentrated in the Red Hill–Main Ridge–Merricks triangle. The most productive pattern for a single Peninsula day: arrive at a 12pm lunch sitting at one of the two-hat venues, allow three hours at the table, then spend the afternoon at cellar doors within 15 minutes: Stonier, Port Phillip Estate, Montalto, Foxeys Hangout, and Yabby Lake are all nearby.

Barragunda and RACV Cape Schanck are the southern outliers. Combine Barragunda with Cape Schanck lighthouse and a night at the Resort if you're making the full drive.

How to Plan a Peninsula Weekend: The Decision Framework
Stop googling. Start here. A step-by-step planning guide that turns 'we should go to the Peninsula' into an actual weekend, with the decisions in the right order.
A notebook and coffee on a table with a Peninsula map and vineyard views through the window — representative image
A decision-framework article for planning a Mornington Peninsula weekend, structured around the questions that actually matter rather than comprehensive venue listings.
The decisions covered in order: length of trip (one vs two nights), which part of the Peninsula, where to stay, what the anchor experience is, what to book first.
The editorial argument: most Peninsula weekend planning fails because people make decisions in the wrong order (accommodation before knowing the area, restaurant before knowing the date).
Suits: any visitor planning their first or second Peninsula trip; couples and groups at the 'we should go' stage who need structure rather than more options.
Planning note: the article recommends booking the one most-wanted hatted restaurant first, then finding accommodation within 15 minutes of it. Written as a framework, not a shortlist.
What is the most important booking to make for a Mornington Peninsula weekend?

The anchor meal — the Saturday lunch or dinner the weekend is built around. Book it before the accommodation if necessary. Peninsula Hot Springs and Alba also require advance booking (3–4 weeks in peak season). Everything else can flex around those two bookings.
How far in advance should I book a Mornington Peninsula weekend?

Accommodation: 4–8 weeks for peak season (December–February, Easter, school holidays). Hatted restaurant lunches: 4–6 weeks for weekends. Peninsula Hot Springs and Alba: 3–4 weeks for weekend sessions. Cellar doors, galleries, and beaches require no advance booking.
How much does a Mornington Peninsula weekend cost?

A mid-range couple's weekend with one night's accommodation and one hatted lunch runs approximately $800–1,200 all-in. A splurge version (Jackalope or Lindenderry, hatted dinner) runs $1,500–2,500. Family rentals with casual dining are typically $500–900.

The Peninsula weekend dies in the planning phase more often than it dies on the road.

Someone suggests it on a Tuesday. Everyone agrees. Then comes the research, a dozen winery websites, an accommodation search that returns three hundred results, a restaurant that requires booking six weeks ahead, a hot springs session that only has a 7am slot, and a growing suspicion that the whole thing is too complicated to organise before Friday.

Most Peninsula weekends that never happen were killed by decision paralysis, not by logistics. The region has too many options, presented in no particular order, with no framework for choosing between them. This guide provides the framework.

There are five decisions. Make them in this order.

## Decision one: who is coming?

This is the decision that determines everything else, and it is the one people make last instead of first.

**A couple.** The Peninsula's default format. The wine-and-food weekend, the anniversary, the escape from the children. This version optimises for one great dinner, one great lunch, a cellar door circuit, and a stay somewhere with a view and a fireplace. Budget: $600–1,200 for the weekend.

**A family.** Different trip entirely. The version that works has one anchor activity per day (gondola, beach, farm), a lunch that tolerates children, and accommodation with a kitchen so you can cook dinner instead of managing a restaurant with tired kids. Budget: $400–900.

**A group of friends.** The Peninsula group weekend works when someone takes charge of the plan. The critical decision: one shared dinner at a long table, everything else loosely coordinated. Six adults rarely stay on the same schedule for a full weekend, and the trip is better for it. Budget: $200–400 per person.

**Solo.** The underrated Peninsula trip. A long walk, a counter lunch, a cellar door tasting where you can talk to the winemaker without a group dynamic. The Peninsula solo day is covered in our [four-hour guide](/journal/the-four-hour-peninsula). Budget: $100–250.

## Decision two: where to stay

The accommodation decision locks in your geography for the weekend. Make it early because it constrains everything else.

**The hinterland (Red Hill, Main Ridge, Merricks).** Stay here if the weekend is about food and wine. You will be within fifteen minutes of the best restaurants, the cellar doors, and the producer trail. The mornings are misty, the evenings are quiet, and the landscape is vineyard and bushland. Options: **Lindenderry** (country house), **Jackalope** (design hotel), **Polperro Villas** or **Crittenden Villas** (vineyard cottages), or Airbnb rentals in the Red Hill area.

**The coast (Sorrento, Portsea).** Stay here if the weekend is about the beach, the village atmosphere, and the view. You will be further from the wineries but closer to the ocean, the ferry, and Point Nepean. **Hotel Sorrento** for the village centre, **The Continental** for the upgrade, rental houses along the cliff for the view.

**The bay side (Mornington, Mount Martha, Dromana).** The cheaper option and the one that works best for families. Closer to Melbourne, closer to the freeway, and the bay beaches are gentler for children. Holiday rentals in Dromana and Rosebud are significantly cheaper than the hinterland or the coast.

**The quiet side (Flinders, Balnarring, Shoreham).** The option for repeat visitors who want silence. Fewer dining options, fewer crowds, better light, and a feeling of being genuinely away. **Flinders Hotel** for a pub stay, rental houses for privacy.

Book the accommodation before the restaurants. The restaurants will adjust to your location; your location will not adjust to the restaurants.

## Decision three: the anchor meal

Every Peninsula weekend has one anchor meal, the lunch or dinner that the trip is organised around. Choose it next.

**For a Saturday lunch:** The Peninsula's best format. The restaurants are at their liveliest, the kitchens are fully staffed, and a long Saturday lunch followed by an afternoon of nothing is the experience the region was built to deliver.

- **Ten Minutes by Tractor.** Fixed menu, vineyard dining room, precise seasonal cooking, one of the Peninsula's most respected kitchens. Book two to four weeks ahead. The anchor meal for a couple or a small group.
- **Montalto.** Warmer, more accessible, with a sculpture trail and a view. Book one to two weeks ahead. Works for families and groups.
- **Tedesca Osteria.** Brigitte Hafner's wood-oven cooking in a farmhouse dining room. Better in winter than summer. Book early.
- **Port Phillip Estate / Pt Leo Estate.** Two sister properties with serious dining rooms and coastal views. The more formal end of the Peninsula lunch.
- **Rare Hare** at Willow Creek. A vineyard bistro that handles a group lunch with more flexibility than the fine-dining options.

**For a Saturday dinner:** Fewer options than lunch, because the Peninsula's dining scene runs on daylight. **Doot Doot Doot** at Jackalope is the dedicated evening restaurant. **Hotel Sorrento** and **The Continental** serve dinner. **Paringa Estate** does Friday and Saturday evenings.

**For a Sunday lunch:** The exit meal. Something relaxed on the way home. **Merricks General Wine Store** for pizza and local wine. **Commonfolk** in Mornington for coffee and a light meal. **Montalto** if you want to repeat the Saturday format at a calmer tempo.

Book the anchor meal before anything else. Everything on the weekend bends around it.

## Decision four: the experiences

With accommodation and the anchor meal locked in, fill the remaining time. The rule: no more than two planned activities per day beyond meals.

**Morning moves (before lunch):**
- **Arthurs Seat Eagle**, gondola to the summit (1 hour)
- A cellar door, **Polperro**, **Montalto**, or **Crittenden** (45 minutes each)
- A producer visit, **Red Hill Cheese**, **Main Ridge Dairy** (30 minutes)
- **Red Hill Market**, first Saturday of the month only (1–2 hours)
- **Alba Thermal Springs** or **Peninsula Hot Springs**, morning session (2 hours including drive)

## Decision five: the logistics

The decisions that people agonise over but shouldn't.

**When to leave Melbourne.** Friday evening if you are staying over, or Saturday by 9am if you are doing a day trip. **How much to book.** Book the accommodation and the anchor meal. Everything else can be walk-in, spontaneous, or decided on the morning. The Peninsula rewards flexibility more than planning.

**What to pack.** Walking shoes, a jacket (the ridge is cooler than Melbourne even in summer), swimmers, a cooler bag for producer purchases, and a corkscrew. If staying in a rental, bring breakfast supplies, the nearest good café might be twenty minutes away.

The Peninsula weekend dies in the planning phase more often than it dies on the road.

Someone suggests it on a Tuesday. Everyone agrees. Then comes the research, a dozen winery websites, an accommodation search that returns three hundred results, a restaurant that requires booking six weeks ahead, a hot springs session that only has a 7am slot, and a growing suspicion that the whole thing is too complicated to organise before Friday.

Most Peninsula weekends that never happen were killed by decision paralysis, not by logistics. The region has too many options, presented in no particular order, with no framework for choosing between them. This guide provides the framework.

There are five decisions. Make them in this order.

Decision one: who is coming?

This is the decision that determines everything else, and it is the one people make last instead of first.

A couple. The Peninsula’s default format. The wine-and-food weekend, the anniversary, the escape from the children. This version optimises for one great dinner, one great lunch, a cellar door circuit, and a stay somewhere with a view and a fireplace. Budget: $600–1,200 for the weekend.

A family. Different trip entirely. The version that works has one anchor activity per day (gondola, beach, farm), a lunch that tolerates children, and accommodation with a kitchen so you can cook dinner instead of managing a restaurant with tired kids. Budget: $400–900.

A group of friends. The Peninsula group weekend works when someone takes charge of the plan. The critical decision: one shared dinner at a long table, everything else loosely coordinated. Six adults rarely stay on the same schedule for a full weekend, and the trip is better for it. Budget: $200–400 per person.

Solo. The underrated Peninsula trip. A long walk, a counter lunch, a cellar door tasting where you can talk to the winemaker without a group dynamic. The Peninsula solo day is covered in our four-hour guide. Budget: $100–250.

Decision two: where to stay

The accommodation decision locks in your geography for the weekend. Make it early because it constrains everything else.

The hinterland (Red Hill, Main Ridge, Merricks). Stay here if the weekend is about food and wine. You will be within fifteen minutes of the best restaurants, the cellar doors, and the producer trail. The mornings are misty, the evenings are quiet, and the landscape is vineyard and bushland. Options: Lindenderry (country house), Jackalope (design hotel), Polperro Villas or Crittenden Villas (vineyard cottages), or Airbnb rentals in the Red Hill area.

The coast (Sorrento, Portsea). Stay here if the weekend is about the beach, the village atmosphere, and the view. You will be further from the wineries but closer to the ocean, the ferry, and Point Nepean. Hotel Sorrento for the village centre, The Continental for the upgrade, rental houses along the cliff for the view.

The bay side (Mornington, Mount Martha, Dromana). The cheaper option and the one that works best for families. Closer to Melbourne, closer to the freeway, and the bay beaches are gentler for children. Holiday rentals in Dromana and Rosebud are significantly cheaper than the hinterland or the coast.

The quiet side (Flinders, Balnarring, Shoreham). The option for repeat visitors who want silence. Fewer dining options, fewer crowds, better light, and a feeling of being genuinely away. Flinders Hotel for a pub stay, rental houses for privacy.

Book the accommodation before the restaurants. The restaurants will adjust to your location; your location will not adjust to the restaurants.

Decision three: the anchor meal

Every Peninsula weekend has one anchor meal, the lunch or dinner that the trip is organised around. Choose it next.

For a Saturday lunch: The Peninsula’s best format. The restaurants are at their liveliest, the kitchens are fully staffed, and a long Saturday lunch followed by an afternoon of nothing is the experience the region was built to deliver.

  • Ten Minutes by Tractor. Fixed menu, vineyard dining room, precise seasonal cooking, one of the Peninsula’s most respected kitchens. Book two to four weeks ahead. The anchor meal for a couple or a small group.
  • Montalto. Warmer, more accessible, with a sculpture trail and a view. Book one to two weeks ahead. Works for families and groups.
  • Tedesca Osteria. Brigitte Hafner’s wood-oven cooking in a farmhouse dining room. Better in winter than summer. Book early.
  • Port Phillip Estate / Pt Leo Estate. Two sister properties with serious dining rooms and coastal views. The more formal end of the Peninsula lunch.
  • Rare Hare at Willow Creek. A vineyard bistro that handles a group lunch with more flexibility than the fine-dining options.

For a Saturday dinner: Fewer options than lunch, because the Peninsula’s dining scene runs on daylight. Doot Doot Doot at Jackalope is the dedicated evening restaurant. Hotel Sorrento and The Continental serve dinner. Paringa Estate does Friday and Saturday evenings.

For a Sunday lunch: The exit meal. Something relaxed on the way home. Merricks General Wine Store for pizza and local wine. Commonfolk in Mornington for coffee and a light meal. Montalto if you want to repeat the Saturday format at a calmer tempo.

Book the anchor meal before anything else. Everything on the weekend bends around it.

HPR Wines: A quiet cellar-door lead best treated as a second-stop prospect

HPR Wines sits in the long tail of Peninsula wine addresses that do not advertise themselves loudly. That usually means either a small producer worth seeking out or a venue whose current public access needs checking before you commit the drive.
HPR Wines vineyard and cellar-door setting on the Mornington Peninsula
What is HPR Wines known for?

Public information on HPR Wines is thinner than it is for the Peninsula's headline estates, and that usually tells you something useful straight away. It reads as a smaller-scale cellar door, a private tasting setup, or a venue whose best use is for readers who already know why they are going.

Some of the Peninsula's most interesting wine experiences sit behind modest websites, irregular opening hours, and a phone-first booking culture. It does change the recommendation though. HPR Wines is not the kind of place to send a first-time visitor without a little homework first.

## Why it may still be worth your time

The reason to keep venues like this on the list is simple: the Peninsula works best when it is not reduced to the same handful of big estates. Smaller operators often give you the part that matters most: a clearer sense of who made the wine, what scale they work at, and whether the visit is actually about the bottle rather than the backdrop.

If HPR Wines is open for tastings when you want to go, expect a visit that is tighter, quieter, and more specific than the region's major hospitality estates. That is usually a good sign.

### How to approach the visit

Treat HPR Wines as a call-ahead address. Worth confirming current access, tasting format, and whether the venue is set up for walk-ins before building a day around it. If the answer is yes, slot it in as one of two stops (not five) and keep lunch elsewhere. That structure gives smaller producers room to be what they are good at.

## How it fits

For readers who like discovering low-profile Peninsula producers, HPR Wines is worth keeping on the working list. For first-timers chasing the cleanest possible day out, it is better used as a second-trip address after the regional benchmarks are covered.

### What to confirm before you drive

Check whether tastings are by appointment, whether wine sales are direct-to-door only, and whether the venue is operating as a true public cellar door at the moment. Small Peninsula wineries change rhythm seasonally and not all of them update that rhythm clearly online.

## What you need to know

- **Status:** Needs verification before visit.
- **Best for:** Readers who prefer smaller producers to polished estates.
- **Approach:** Contact first, then fold it into a two-stop day.
- **Location:** Mornington Peninsula, Mornington Peninsula region.
- **Bottom line:** Interesting enough to keep on the radar, not yet confirmed enough to recommend blindly.

Insider Picks — Week of 14 May: Four Moves Before Winter Sets In
One booking to lock in this week, one move for tonight, one walk while the light holds, and one autumn lunch in a room that is currently as quiet as it gets.
Late-autumn light on the southern coast of the Mornington Peninsula
Tedesca, Tractor, Laura: The Three Peninsula Dinners
When does Red Hill Truffles open for 2026?

Red Hill Truffles' Périgord black truffle season runs from Saturday 30 May 2026 through to the end of September. The hunt and pizza option ($189pp, 3 hours) is the most flexible on lead time. The two premium hunts — Truffle Hunt × Red Hill Estate Restaurant ($199 adults, includes a two-course truffle lunch) and Truffle Hunt & Gourmet Lunch at The Epicurean Red Hill ($195pp) — book out four to six weeks ahead and should be locked in this week if you want a June or July date.
What is on at Peninsula Hot Springs on Thursday nights in May 2026?

Bathe-in Cinema runs Thursday evenings at the Peninsula Hot Springs amphitheatre pool throughout May, June, and July 2026. You watch the film from inside a thermal pool. A bathing-session ticket is required; the amphitheatre fills early; check the PHS events page for the week's film. Better in mid-autumn and winter than it is in summer — the cold air is the point.

This is the second-to-last week before winter framing starts to feel earned. The forecast is doing us a favour — 14 to 20 °C, sunny, light wind, dry through at least Saturday. Mother's Day is done. King's Birthday is still four weekends away. The Peninsula is in one of its rare uncrowded, unbusy in-between windows, and the rooms that were impossible in April are answering the phone.

Four picks. One for this week, one for tonight, one for whichever afternoon you can spare, and one for the long lunch you keep saying you'll book and don't.

## 1. Book the truffle hunt this week

**Red Hill Truffles. Season opens Saturday 30 May. 1180 Mornington-Flinders Road, Main Ridge. From $189pp.**

This is the only genuinely time-sensitive pick on the list.

Red Hill Truffles runs three public hunt formats through the Périgord season. The Truffle Hunt and Pizza option, three hours, $189 per person, is the forgiving one and tends to have availability into the season. The two we'd actually book — Truffle Hunt × Red Hill Estate Restaurant at $199 per person, and Truffle Hunt and Gourmet Lunch at The Epicurean Red Hill at $195 per person — fill four to six weeks ahead. June Saturdays are already tight. July long-weekend dates almost always go first.

If you want a hunt during the King's Birthday weekend (5 to 8 June), book this week. After Sunday it stops being a choice and starts being a question of what is left.

## 2. Tonight: Bathe-in Cinema at Peninsula Hot Springs

**Thursday 14 May. Amphitheatre pool, Peninsula Hot Springs, 140 Springs Lane, Rye. Bathing-session ticket required.**

The mid-May version of this is the one to do. The water is warm, the air is finally cold enough to make the contrast read as the gimmick it was always meant to be, and the amphitheatre pool — the only one with line of sight to the screen — fills earlier than people expect.

The pick is not the film. The film changes week to week. The pick is the format: an outdoor thermal pool, the dark, and a screen, on a Thursday night when nothing else is on. The cinema sessions run weekly through July. May is when they start being worth choosing over a regular evening bathing session.

Book the late session. Check the lineup at peninsulahotsprings.com before you commit.

## 3. Use the light while it holds — Bushrangers Bay

**90 minutes, moderate. Trailhead at the Cape Schanck lighthouse precinct, Cape Schanck Road.**

The forecast is genuinely good through Saturday. Sunset is around 17:25. Start the walk at 15:30 and you arrive at the bay with the sun low enough to silver across the basalt.

Bushrangers Bay is the walk we send people to when they want the wilder Peninsula without committing to a full-day hike. The track drops out of the lighthouse precinct through coastal scrub and opens onto a wide crescent of dark sand and rock stacks. The return climb is sharp enough to justify a coffee or an early dinner inland afterwards, but not so punishing that it tips into a chore.

May is the best month for this walk. The summer haze is gone, the crowds are absent on a weekday, and the late afternoon light flattens the southern coastline into something that does not photograph as well as it lives.

If the weather flips before Saturday, the back-up is the Cape Schanck boardwalk — short, paved, the same coastline at a quarter of the commitment.

## 4. The long autumn lunch you keep meaning to book

**Paringa Estate, 44 Paringa Road, Red Hill South — or — Tedesca Osteria, 96 Junction Road, Red Hill.**

This is the lunch room the calendar is currently giving you for free.

Two weeks ago every serious Peninsula lunch was buried under Mother's Day. Three weeks from now they will be buried under King's Birthday. This week, and probably next, are the cleanest mid-autumn long-lunch windows the Peninsula sees all year. Quiet rooms. No occasion premium. Produce at peak — mushrooms early in their run, the last of the autumn pinot pours, kitchens settling back into single-sitting service.

Pick one room. We won't push you between them.

**Paringa Estate** if you want the wine to be the headline. Lindsay McCall planted his first vines in 1985 and the 'LJM' Pinot Noir is one of the Peninsula's benchmark bottles. One-hat restaurant, smart compact cellar door, terrace that earns its hours of sun on a clear autumn afternoon. The least theatrical of the serious Peninsula rooms.

**Tedesca Osteria** if you want the room to be the point. Brigitte Hafner's farmhouse osteria, two hats, one set menu, single sitting for lunch. The wood oven runs all service. Pasta is rolled in the morning. The garden feeds half the menu. Book a fortnight out for a weekend table; mid-week is currently easier.

Either one. Lunch over dinner. Single venue, no driving after.

Paringa Estate, 44 Paringa Road, Red Hill South — or — Tedesca Osteria, 96 Junction Road, Red Hill.

This is the lunch room the calendar is currently giving you for free.

Two weeks ago every serious Peninsula lunch was buried under Mother’s Day. Three weeks from now they will be buried under King’s Birthday. This week, and probably next, are the cleanest mid-autumn long-lunch windows the Peninsula sees all year. Quiet rooms. No occasion premium. Produce at peak — mushrooms early in their run, the last of the autumn pinot pours, kitchens settling back into single-sitting service.

Pick one room. We won’t push you between them.

Paringa Estate if you want the wine to be the headline. Lindsay McCall planted his first vines in 1985 and the ‘LJM’ Pinot Noir is one of the Peninsula’s benchmark bottles. One-hat restaurant, smart compact cellar door, terrace that earns its hours of sun on a clear autumn afternoon. The least theatrical of the serious Peninsula rooms.

Tedesca Osteria if you want the room to be the point. Brigitte Hafner’s farmhouse osteria, two hats, one set menu, single sitting for lunch. The wood oven runs all service. Pasta is rolled in the morning. The garden feeds half the menu. Book a fortnight out for a weekend table; mid-week is currently easier.

Either one. Lunch over dinner. Single venue, no driving after.

This edition picks for that register. Different walks, different rooms, a closing cultural window that won't be here in three weeks, and one booking that has a hard deadline.

## Lock in the final forage before Sunday

**Wild Mushroom Forage and Lunch with The Kitchen. Saturday 30 May, 11am–1:30pm. $85 per person. Red Hill and Main Ridge forests. Strictly capped at 15.**

The session this Saturday (May 23) is covered in the weekend dispatch. This pick is about the one after it.

Saturday 30 May is the final session of the season. The format is the same: a guide with fifteen-plus years behind them, a two-hour walk through the Red Hill and Main Ridge forests looking for the edible wild mushrooms that come up after the autumn rains, then the cook-up on the spot. Butter, herbs, warm bread, what the morning found. Fifteen people maximum, no exceptions.

The Kitchen takes no online bookings. Contact them directly. If this week passes without a booking, it becomes the question of what is left.

The timing note: there is one more session on the calendar after the forage closes. Red Hill Truffles season opens the same morning, Saturday 30 May. If you book the forage and the truffle hunt in the same week, you have earned a serious late-autumn weekend.

## The walk for this weather

**Greens Bush (Two Bays section). Greens Bush Carpark, off Baldrys Road, Merricks North. 4 hours, moderate.**

Last week's pick was about coastal light. This week's is about everything the Peninsula has when the light goes grey.

Greens Bush is 8.9 kilometres one-way through the largest remnant bushland on the Mornington Peninsula. The canopy closes overhead in places, old grasstrees — some over two hundred years old — stand through the fern gullies and tea-tree, and the track passes through a landscape that looks largely as it would have before European settlement. Birds work the understory constantly. You will hear more than you see.

The walk is autumn and winter best, not despite the overcast but partly because of it. The light is even, the colours are sharp, and the crowds that make Point Nepean and Cape Schanck feel compressed on a clear-sky Saturday are not here.

Walk it as a return circuit from the Greens Bush Carpark or do the full one-way with a car shuffle and someone else's opinion about where to eat at the other end. Merricks General Wine Store is the nearest reasonable stop.

## Two weeks left — Tall Poppy, Moorooduc

**Kelli Lundberg Art @ The Studio & Co., Moorooduc. Closes 7 June. Free entry, no booking.**

The claim with Tall Poppy is that it is the first time NGV's Melbourne Design Week has programmed an exhibition on the Mornington Peninsula. The Melbourne Design Week 2026 catalogue corroborates it. Whether or not the claim holds exactly, the show is worth the drive for independent reasons.

Fifteen Australian designers and makers: furniture, ceramics, textiles, design objects. Curated by Tiffany Jade, who works from inside the same Studio & Co. precinct — a converted 1920s grocery building in Moorooduc with twenty-plus maker tenants. The space is working creative infrastructure, not a white-cube gallery. You will likely find people actually making things while you look at the show.

The show closes 7 June. Two weekends of life remain. The natural Saturday: lunch on the Red Hill ridge, then down to Moorooduc for the exhibition in the early afternoon. Accessibility is notably well-considered for a regional venue: wheelchair access, accessible bathrooms, online viewing option.

Open most days 10am to 4pm. 10am to 3pm Sundays. Closed Tuesdays. Parking via Derril Road.

## The dinner for this moment

**Tedesca Osteria, 96 Junction Road, Red Hill.**

There are two versions of Tedesca. The terrace version, which earns its two hats in the warm months on a clear Peninsula afternoon. And the winter version, which earns them a different way: wood-oven heat, a set menu that runs on what the cold season actually offers, a room that is warm in the particular way that rooms with kitchens in them are warm.

This week is the transition point. The terrace is no longer the draw. The room is.

Brigitte Hafner's kitchen runs on produce and wood and the kind of cooking that does not announce itself. The set menu means you have given up control, which is the correct call. Book three to four weeks ahead for King's Birthday if that is the plan; for a quieter mid-week or non-occasion Saturday, earlier availability is usually there.

The booking: tedescasteria.com.au. The room is small. Give it the first call of the week.

Jones Road: A Peninsula producer to verify before you build the day around it

Jones Road sits in the long tail of Peninsula wine addresses that do not advertise themselves loudly. That usually means either a small producer worth seeking out or a venue whose current public access needs checking before you commit the drive.
Jones Road vineyard and cellar-door setting on the Mornington Peninsula
What is Jones Road known for?

Public information on Jones Road is thinner than it is for the Peninsula's headline estates, and that usually tells you something useful straight away. It reads as a smaller-scale producer, a private tasting setup, or a venue whose best use is for readers who already know why they are going.

Some of the Peninsula's most interesting wine experiences sit behind modest websites, irregular opening hours, and a phone-first booking culture. It does change the recommendation though. Jones Road is not the kind of place to send a first-time visitor without a little homework first.

## Why it may still be worth your time

The reason to keep venues like this on the list is simple: the Peninsula works best when it is not reduced to the same handful of big estates. Smaller operators often give you the part that matters most: a clearer sense of who made the wine, what scale they work at, and whether the visit is actually about the bottle rather than the backdrop.

If Jones Road is open for tastings when you want to go, expect a visit that is tighter, quieter, and more specific than the region's major hospitality estates. That is usually a good sign.

### How to approach the visit

Treat Jones Road as a call-ahead address. Worth confirming current access, tasting format, and whether the venue is set up for walk-ins before building a day around it. If the answer is yes, slot it in as one of two stops (not five) and keep lunch elsewhere. That structure gives smaller producers room to be what they are good at.

## How it fits

For readers who like discovering low-profile Peninsula producers, Jones Road is worth keeping on the working list. For first-timers chasing the cleanest possible day out, it is better used as a second-trip address after the regional benchmarks are covered.

### What to confirm before you drive

Check whether tastings are by appointment, whether wine sales are direct-to-door only, and whether the venue is operating as a true public cellar door at the moment. Small Peninsula wineries change rhythm seasonally and not all of them update that rhythm clearly online.

Luxury Hotels on the Mornington Peninsula — The Honest Guide

One MICHELIN Two Keys hotel, one IHG five-star on a clifftop, and a country house hotel with two AGFG hats. Plus the most common confusion on the Peninsula: Hotel Sorrento and InterContinental Sorrento are not the same property.
Jackalope Hotel, Merricks North — a MICHELIN Two Keys property and one of the Peninsula's flagship luxury stays
Peninsula Hot Springs vs Alba (Spa Stays)
The Best Spas on the Mornington Peninsula
What is the best luxury hotel on the Mornington Peninsula?

Jackalope Hotel in Merricks North holds the MICHELIN Two Keys designation (2025) — among the first Australian properties to receive this award. 45 rooms, vineyard infinity pool, two hatted restaurants (Doot Doot Doot and Rare Hare). No children under 12. For a different character of luxury, InterContinental Sorrento at 23 Constitution Hill Road is a full-service IHG five-star with a heated clifftop bay-view pool and Aurora Spa & Bathhouse, built on the site of the 1875 Continental Hotel.
What is the difference between Hotel Sorrento and InterContinental Sorrento?

They are completely separate properties — different buildings, different streets, different ownership. Hotel Sorrento is at 5–15 Hotham Road: a boutique pub hotel with a five-year renovation completed January 2026 and Shi Hui Shi Cantonese restaurant in its limestone basement. InterContinental Sorrento is at 23 Constitution Hill Road: the IHG five-star that opened August 2022 after a $100M+ redevelopment of the original 1875 Continental Hotel. Do not book one expecting the other.
Are there luxury hotels near Peninsula Hot Springs?

The closest luxury option to Peninsula Hot Springs is the Alba Sanctuary at 282 Browns Road, Fingal — five hilltop villas plus two premium rooms, adults-only (18+), from $624/night, with access to the 22 geothermal pools at Alba Thermal Springs. On the same site as Peninsula Hot Springs itself, the Glamping & Eco Lodges include premium eco lodges with geothermal floor heating and full spa complex access.

No children under 12 are permitted at Jackalope Hotel. For luxury family accommodation, RACV Cape Schanck Resort (184 rooms, championship golf, multiple dining) is the best full-service option on the Peninsula.

## One clarification before anything else

**Hotel Sorrento** (5–15 Hotham Road) and **InterContinental Sorrento** (23 Constitution Hill Road) are completely separate properties. This confusion affects more bookings than almost any other issue on the Peninsula.

Hotel Sorrento is a boutique pub hotel that completed a five-year renovation in January 2026. InterContinental Sorrento is an IHG five-star that opened August 2022 on the site of the 1875 Continental Hotel (known locally as "The Conti"). Different buildings, different streets, different ownership, different price points.

Every piece of copy about either property should state the street address clearly.

---

## Tier 1: MICHELIN and five-star

### Jackalope Hotel, Merricks North
Australia's MICHELIN Two Keys property. 45 rooms on the Willow Creek Vineyard estate. The designation, awarded in 2025, recognises Jackalope's position in international hospitality; the first Australian properties received it in 2025 and there are very few.

The hotel: vineyard infinity pool, heated spa, infrared sauna, deep-soak Japanese baths in Lair and Vineyard Bath rooms. No children under 12.

The food is a legitimate part of the stay: Doot Doot Doot (dinner nightly, one hat GFG 2025) and Rare Hare (walk-in, outdoor wood-fired, one hat GFG 2025) are both worth booking regardless of whether you're staying.

From approximately $400–600+/night. Minimum two-night stay on weekends likely. Verify current rates.

166 Balnarring Road, Merricks North. [jackalopehotels.com](https://jackalopehotels.com)

### InterContinental Sorrento, Sorrento (23 Constitution Hill Road)
IHG five-star on the clifftop above Sorrento. Opened August 2022 after a $100M+ redevelopment of the site that's housed a hotel since 1875. Heated outdoor bay-view pool with cabanas. Aurora Spa & Bathhouse with thermal bathing pools and a full treatment menu. CeeCee's all-day dining plus the Pool Deck Bar. Minimum check-in age 18.

The location (clifftop above Sorrento, walking distance to the village) is among the best of any hotel on the Peninsula.

From approximately $595/night (2022 launch pricing; verify current). Website: [thecontinentalsorrento.com.au](https://thecontinentalsorrento.com.au)

*Note: completely separate from Hotel Sorrento at 5–15 Hotham Road.*

### RACV Cape Schanck Resort, Cape Schanck
The Peninsula's largest resort, 184 rooms. Five-star RACV property adjacent to the Cape Schanck lighthouse. Championship golf course on-site (one of two courses at Moonah Links). One Spa (massage, facials, hammam). Four dining venues: Cape, Samphire, Mantellina, and Cape Bar & Terrace. RACV member benefits apply.

A strong fit for families and groups who want full resort facilities. The only hotel with golf course on-site.

[racv.com.au](https://racv.com.au)

---

## Tier 1B: High-end boutique

### Lancemore Lindenderry Red Hill, Red Hill
40 rooms in a country house hotel format. The Dining Room holds two hats in the AGFG 2025/2026; dinner Thursday to Saturday, lunch Friday to Sunday. Lake views, tall silver birch trees, formal gardens. Recognised by Luxury Travel Magazine as one of Australia's most romantic regional hotels. From approximately $300–600+/night.

The AGFG recognition makes this a more serious food destination than its country-house aesthetic might suggest.

142 Arthurs Seat Road, Red Hill. [lancemore.com.au](https://lancemore.com.au)

### Hotel Sorrento, Sorrento (5–15 Hotham Road)
Boutique pub hotel. 150+ year history, five-year renovation completed January 2026. Outdoor pool. Shi Hui Shi Cantonese restaurant in the limestone basement; chef Junlin Yi (ex-Red Spice Road). From approximately $309/night. Four-star.

*Note: completely separate from InterContinental Sorrento at 23 Constitution Hill Road.*

[hotelsorrento.com.au](https://hotelsorrento.com.au)

---

## Spa and thermal spring stays

### Alba Sanctuary, Fingal
The accommodation arm of Alba Thermal Springs. Five hilltop villas plus two premium rooms, all adults-only (minimum age 18). Access to the 22-pool geothermal complex on-site. Slippers, robes, complimentary minibar included. From $624/night. Five minutes from Peninsula Hot Springs.

282 Browns Road, Fingal. [albathermalsprings.com.au](https://www.albathermalsprings.com.au)

---

## How to choose

**For a design-led food-and-wine stay:** Jackalope Hotel, particularly if MICHELIN recognition matters and budget is not the constraint.

**For a heritage clifftop hotel with full service:** InterContinental Sorrento: five-star, IHG points, Aurora Spa, central for exploring the Sorrento tip.

**For families:** RACV Cape Schanck Resort, the resort on the Peninsula with the scale to absorb children, golfers, and spa-seeking adults simultaneously.

**For a romantic long-weekend with a serious dinner:** Lancemore Lindenderry; the Dining Room is hatted, and the setting matches it.

**For spa-first travellers near the hot springs:** Alba Sanctuary: on-site geothermal access and the most resolved thermal-spring accommodation on the Peninsula.

*Last fact-verified: 22 April 2026.*


*Prices may change. Confirm current rates directly with the venue or operator before booking.*

The Mornington Day: How to Treat the Gateway Town as the Destination
Forget pressing on to the vineyards. A well-built day in Mornington  -  market, coffee, gallery, foreshore  -  is one of the cleanest Peninsula visits you can make.
Mornington main street with morning shoppers and cafes — representative image
A complete day-trip guide to Mornington town — structured to make the most of the Peninsula's main hub in a single day without a car-heavy itinerary.
Covers: the Wednesday market as the ideal starting point; the foreshore walk; the best café and lunch options; what the main street actually offers beyond coffee.
The editorial argument: Mornington is consistently underused as a destination in its own right rather than a gateway town. This piece treats it as the destination.
Suits: day-trippers from Melbourne; visitors staying in Mount Martha or nearby who want a full Mornington day; anyone who has dismissed Mornington as 'just a service town'.
Planning note: Wednesday is the best day by a significant margin (market day). Parking fills quickly near the market from 8:30am. The Esplanade walk is the correct way to close the day.
What should I do on a day trip to Mornington?

Coffee at Commonfolk, the main street loop (gallery, shops, foreshore), lunch at Bass and Flinders Distillery or a Main Street bistro, then Mount Martha Beach in the afternoon. Four stops in roughly six hours — no wasted driving, and walkable between most of them.
When is the Mornington Farmers' Market?

Second Saturday of each month on the Esplanade bayfront. It's the best monthly market on the Peninsula for produce, cheese, bread, and local goods — worth structuring a whole day around if you're coming in the morning.
Is Mornington worth visiting on its own, or should I continue to Red Hill?

Worth a full day on its own — gallery, market, foreshore, good coffee, and Mount Martha Beach. If you want wineries and cellar doors, Red Hill is a separate day. Trying to combine both usually ends with rushing everything and enjoying neither.

Mornington has a problem and the problem is geography. It is the first stop on the Peninsula when you drive down from Melbourne, and for a long time that meant nobody stayed: you bought a coffee, stretched your legs, and pressed on to the wineries or the tip. The town became a waypoint by default.

That is now a lazy reading. Over the past decade Mornington has evolved into one of the most complete day-out towns on the Peninsula. It has a genuinely good main street, a monthly farmers' market on the bayfront, a regional gallery that punches well above its weight, and a short drive in either direction to serious food or serious beaches. Built right, a Mornington day is cleaner and less expensive than a Red Hill day and often just as satisfying.


## 9:00: Start at Commonfolk

**Commonfolk Coffee** is the town's best roaster and the best place to begin the day. The roastery is tucked into an industrial backstreet off Progress Street (worth the small detour) and the cafe out the front serves the coffee the rest of the Peninsula is trying to match. Order a filter from the single-origin rotation, then walk the retail wall before you leave.

Breakfast here if you are hungry, but keep it light. The better eating happens later.

## 10:30: The main street loop

Main Street Mornington runs downhill from the clock tower toward the bay. Walk it once north to south without stopping except at the shops that catch your eye: the homewares stores are better than the ones in Red Hill, the bookshop on Main Street is genuinely useful, and the secondhand and vintage places are worth the loop. Drop down to the foreshore at the bottom and walk back along the bay path.

If it is the second Saturday of the month, this is when the **Mornington Farmers' Market** is running in the park on the Esplanade. Bag it in. This is the best monthly market on the Peninsula and it will handle your lunch, your produce for home, and your cheese for dinner.

## 12:30: The gallery

**Mornington Peninsula Regional Gallery** is a ten-minute walk inland from the main street and entry is free. The permanent collection leans Australian modernist; the rotating program usually has a contemporary show worth sitting with. This is the Peninsula's best wet-weather fallback and, more importantly, the move that turns a Mornington day from a brunch-and-shop circuit into something a bit more considered.

Check the program before you go. Allow forty-five minutes minimum.

## 1:30: Lunch somewhere deliberate

The town has improved its food scene without becoming a cellar-door circuit. Main Street has a handful of reliable modern bistros, and for a longer lunch the better move is to drive seven minutes inland to **Bass & Flinders Distillery** in Tuerong for a gin-tasting flight and a short food menu. If the day has gone casual, the foreshore kiosks and the pub lunches along the Esplanade are cheerful and good.

What you don't want to do is drive thirty minutes to a Red Hill cellar door restaurant in the middle of a Mornington day. It breaks the rhythm and the drive back is worse than you think.

## 3:30: Mount Martha

A Mornington day improves the moment you add **Mount Martha Beach** to the end of it. The beach is seven minutes south of town, runs along a long gentle curve of pale sand with the bathing boxes at the northern end, and is the cleanest swim on the Peninsula from late spring through to autumn. If it is too cold for swimming, walk the coastal track from the car park south along the cliff: twenty minutes each way, mostly flat, with the kind of views that remind you why people settled here.

This is the move that closes the day. You come back into town for dinner at 6.30 and you have already had the equivalent of a full weekend.

## Getting the most from your Mornington day

The single biggest error is treating Mornington as a coffee stop on the way to Red Hill. You will fight the traffic, rush the main street, skip the gallery, and arrive at your vineyard restaurant irritated rather than excited. If the day is about wine country, come down on a different day. If the day is about Mornington, let it be about Mornington.

Done properly, it is a slower, gentler, and often more memorable version of a Peninsula visit than the cellar-door circuit. And it is unusually easy to do with children, parents, or anyone else in the group who will not thank you for a four-hour degustation.

The town has earned the visit. Give it the whole day.

Sorrento Ocean Baths on Port Phillip Bay — one of the Peninsula’s most popular beach destinations
Which beach is best for kids on the Mornington Peninsula?

Mothers Beach in Mornington is usually the top pick — sheltered by the pier, shallow, patrolled on select summer days, and close to cafes and playgrounds. Safety Beach, Rye Front and Rosebud are also consistently calm. Avoid any Bass Strait back beach for young children.
Where can I take my dog on the Mornington Peninsula?

Year-round off-leash beaches include Tassells Cove (Safety Beach), Hawker Beach (Mount Martha), Fossil Beach (Mornington), Flinders Beach north end, Somers Beach (with some time-of-day variation), and Anthony's Nose (Dromana). Dogs are not permitted anywhere in the Mornington Peninsula National Park — including every ocean back beach. On Shire-managed bay beaches, dogs are allowed on-leash but prohibited from the sand between 9am and 7pm during daylight saving.
What's the difference between a front beach and a back beach on the Mornington Peninsula?

Front beaches face Port Phillip Bay — calm, shallow, close to the towns. Back beaches face Bass Strait — open ocean, surf, cliffs, strong rip currents. Front beaches are for swimming and paddling; back beaches are for surfing and cliff-top walks (with care).
Is the Two Bays Walk hard?

It's rated Grade 3 (moderate) on the Australian Walking Track Grading Scale — doable in a long day for fit walkers, or split across two days with a night at the Lightwood Creek camping area. The track is 26km one-way from Dromana to Cape Schanck. The harder sections are the climb up Arthurs Seat and the final descent to Cape Schanck. Carry all your water — there are no drinking taps along the trail.

Most visitors arrive on the Mornington Peninsula thinking of "the beach" as one thing. It isn't.

The peninsula has three coastlines, and each one plays by different rules. On the west, Port Phillip Bay laps at calm, shallow "front" beaches that sit beside the towns, Sorrento, Mornington, Mount Martha, Rye, Rosebud. On the south, Bass Strait hammers the "back" beaches, Gunnamatta, Sorrento Back Beach, Portsea Back, Flinders Ocean, a rugged surf coast inside the Mornington Peninsula National Park. On the east, Western Port Bay is quieter again: tidal, low-key, with long stretches of sand at Balnarring, Somers, and Flinders' north end.

Which coastline you want depends on who's with you. A toddler and a paddleboard? Bay. A surfer or a photographer chasing cliffs? Ocean. A dog that needs to run? Almost certainly Western Port or one of the Shire's off-leash zones, because dogs are not permitted anywhere inside Mornington Peninsula National Park.

This is the full guide: where to swim, where to surf, where to walk, what's patrolled, and what's currently closed.

---

## Three coastlines, one peninsula

The shape of the peninsula is the whole story. It's a curving spit of land pointing north-west from Melbourne, separating Port Phillip Bay on one side from the open ocean on the other, with Western Port lapping at its eastern flank.

### Port Phillip Bay: the "front" beaches

These are the beaches most first-time visitors picture: calm, shallow, sandy, with colourful bathing boxes and a pier nearby. Mothers Beach in Mornington is generally flat and calm, the pier's positioning shields it from chop. Further south, Sorrento Front, Rye Front, Rosebud and Safety Beach offer the same protected water: good for young children, paddleboarding, and anyone who doesn't want to deal with surf.

Front beaches are where the Shire's seasonal **beach matting** appears each November, running until around late April or May at Mt Martha, Mornington's Mothers Beach, Rosebud (near the jetty), Rye Front (near the pier) and Sorrento Front (near The Baths). Mount Martha also keeps two floating **MobiChairs** available on weekends during patrol hours, they float, so wheelchairs can enter the water. Call the Mount Martha Life Saving Club on (03) 5974 4140 to confirm current patrol dates.

### Bass Strait: the "back" or ocean beaches

Drive fifteen minutes across the peninsula from Sorrento town and you're in a different country. The ocean beaches sit inside the Mornington Peninsula National Park, with powerful surf, weathered cliffs, and real rip currents. Sorrento Back Beach, Portsea Back, Gunnamatta, Rye Ocean, St Andrews, Koonya, Flinders Ocean, all ocean, all rugged.

Three are **patrolled**, Sorrento Back, Portsea Back and Gunnamatta, on summer weekends and during school holidays only. The rest are unpatrolled; Parks Victoria explicitly advises against swimming at Rye Ocean. Gunnamatta is the most popular surf beach in the National Park and, per Visit Mornington Peninsula, the most hazardous for swimming. Swim between the flags.

**Dogs are not permitted anywhere in the National Park**, not on the beaches, not in the car parks, not in Greens Bush. The management plan was amended in October 2016 and has not changed since.

### Western Port: the quieter east

Western Port is where locals often go when the rest of the peninsula is busy. Balnarring, Somers, Point Leo, Shoreham, Flinders' north end, these beaches are tidal, lower-key, and friendlier to dogs. Flinders Beach's north end, between Dodds Creek and Manton Creek, is off-leash year-round. Tassells Cove at Safety Beach and Hawker Beach at Mount Martha are also year-round off-leash.

---

## Which beaches are patrolled?

| Beach | Coastline | Patrolled by | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sorrento Back Beach | Ocean | Life Saving Victoria | Summer weekends + school holidays |
| Portsea Back Beach | Ocean | Life Saving Victoria | Summer + school holidays |
| Gunnamatta Ocean Beach | Ocean | Life Saving Victoria | Summer + school holidays |
| Mount Martha (south end) | Bay | Mount Martha LSC | Weekends, summer |
| Mornington Main (Mothers) | Bay | Mornington LSC | Select summer days |
| Dromana Beach | Bay | Dromana Bay LSC | Summer |
| Point Leo | Western Port | Point Leo SLSC | Summer |

Ocean beaches not in the table above, Rye Ocean, St Andrews, Koonya, Flinders Ocean, Bushrangers Bay, can still be visited, but swimming is not advised at several of them.

Patrol seasons vary year to year. Check Life Saving Victoria's beach safety feed before any weekend visit.

---

## Where you can (and can't) bring your dog

### Mornington Peninsula National Park: no dogs, ever

Inside the National Park, which includes every ocean back beach plus Greens Bush, dogs are prohibited. On beaches. In car parks. On the Two Bays Walk. There is no seasonal window, no before-9am loophole. This rule was locked in by a management plan amendment in October 2016.

<AlertBlock type="danger" heading="Active alert: PAPP fox baiting">
Fox control baiting with PAPP poison is active from Portsea Ocean Beach through to Greens Bush until October 2026. PAPP is lethal to dogs. If your dog is suspected of having ingested a bait, go to a vet immediately, the antidote is methylene blue.
</AlertBlock>

### Year-round off-leash beaches

Six confirmed year-round off-leash sections: Tassells Cove (Safety Beach), Hawker Beach (Mount Martha), Somers Beach (east of the yacht club, with some time-of-day variation), Fossil Beach (Mornington), Flinders Beach north end (between Dodds Creek and Manton Creek), and Anthony's Nose (Dromana).

### The standard Shire rule

For most other Shire-managed bay beaches, dogs are permitted on-leash. During daylight saving, they're prohibited from the sand between 9am and 7pm. Some beaches apply stricter local zones. Check the Mornington Peninsula Shire's current beach controls before you go, rules change, and Shire signage outranks any travel post.

---

## Current alerts

*Last verified: 22 April 2026. Pull from Parks Victoria's Closures & Current Conditions feed before every publish.*

<AlertBlock type="danger" heading="Flinders Ocean Beach: active landslip">
A landslip west of Mushroom Reef is active. Do not approach the slip. The toilet at Flinders Ocean Beach is also permanently closed. Verify status with Parks Victoria before visiting.
</AlertBlock>

<AlertBlock type="danger" heading="MPNP fox baiting: active until October 2026">
PAPP poison baiting and trapping is underway from Portsea Ocean Beach to Greens Bush. Lethal to dogs. Keep all pets out of the National Park.
</AlertBlock>

<AlertBlock type="warning" heading="Cape Schanck boardwalk: works in progress">

</AlertBlock>

</AlertBlock>

---

## Beaches by town

**Sorrento.** Two completely different beach days, five minutes apart. The Front Beach (bay side) is calm and accessible, a 40m beach ramp near the kiosk is the best wheelchair access on the ocean side of the peninsula. The Back Beach (ocean side) is surfed and photographed; rock pools large enough to swim in at low tide.

**Portsea.** The Front Beach is a scuba-diving hub with historic jetties and boat sheds. The Back Beach runs along weathered Bass Strait cliffs and is patrolled in summer.

**Mount Martha.** A two-kilometre stretch divided by Balcombe Creek. The southern end is patrolled and home to the most accessible beach setup on the bay: daily beach matting, floating MobiChairs on weekends.

**Rye and Rosebud.** Shallow, family-friendly bay beaches. Rye Pier is one of the best snorkelling spots on the peninsula, warm, about 6m deep, regularly occupied by divers. Rosebud has extensive foreshore parklands and BBQs.

**Safety Beach.** Tassells Cove is year-round off-leash and a favourite with locals for exactly that reason.

**Flinders.** Two entirely different beaches sharing one name. Flinders Ocean Beach (Bass Strait side) is a snorkelling and surf spot, currently affected by a landslip west of Mushroom Reef. Flinders Beach (Western Port side) is a 3km stretch with off-leash dog access at the north end.

**Balnarring and Point Leo.** Quieter Western Port beaches. Point Leo is patrolled in summer and sits next to the Point Leo Estate sculpture park.

---

## Walks and outdoor escapes

**Two Bays Walk.** 26km one-way from Dromana foreshore to Cape Schanck (Parks Victoria figure; Trail Hiking Australia and the Two Bays Trail Run commonly cite 28km, a discrepancy we cover in full in the section-by-section guide). Grade 3 moderate. Carry all your water, no drinking taps along the trail. Lightwood Creek camping area sits at the mid-point: five campsites, no fees, no bookings required, max two nights. → [Two Bays Walk guide](/explore/two-bays-walking-track/)

**Cape Schanck boardwalk.** 2.1km return from the carpark to Pulpit Rock and Pebble Beach; allow 45 minutes to an hour. The 1859 lighthouse is at the trailhead. Upgrades currently in progress, check on-site signage. → [Cape Schanck guide](/journal/cape-schanck-guide/)

**Point Nepean National Park.** Entry is free. The Fort Nepean shuttle is around $12 return if you don't want to walk the full route out. Two all-terrain beach wheelchairs and one standard wheelchair are free to borrow from the Information Centre. → [Point Nepean guide](/explore/point-nepean-national-park/)

**Bushrangers Bay.** 5.4km return from the Cape Schanck eastern carpark, about two hours. Spectacular, unpatrolled, and not a swimming beach, Parks Victoria's own language includes "unpredictable rips, strong currents, rocky reefs, large waves" and "limited access for emergency services." Worth every step; not for a swim.

**Greens Bush.** The largest remnant of native bushland on the peninsula, tucked between Arthurs Seat and Cape Schanck. The Two Bays route passes straight through it. 8.9km of the trail runs inside Greens Bush, with circuit options at either end. Phone reception is unreliable, carry a printed map.

---

## Accessibility on the Peninsula's beaches

Five front beaches are fitted with beach matting from late November to the end of April or May:

- **Mt Martha Beach**, daily at the SLSC
- **Mothers Beach, Mornington**, daily
- **Rosebud Beach**, daily near the jetty
- **Rye Front Beach**, near the pier
- **Sorrento Front Beach**, near The Baths

Mount Martha has two floating MobiChairs available during weekend patrol hours, 12–5pm. They float, wheelchairs can enter the water. Phone (03) 5974 4140 to confirm.

On the ocean side, Sorrento Back Beach has a 40m accessible ramp (slope 1:12 then 1:14) near the kiosk, Parks Victoria's own wording calls it the best accessibility access point on the National Park's ocean beaches.

At Point Nepean, the Quarantine Station, Coles Track and Defence Road are accessible. The shuttle bus accommodates standard (not motorised) wheelchairs. Two all-terrain beach wheelchairs and one standard wheelchair are free to borrow from the Information Centre.

## Practical notes

**Parking.** Sorrento Back Beach has a large car park. Portsea Back has four. Gunnamatta has two large car parks off Truemans Road. Front beaches are metered or time-limited in peak season, check Shire signage.

**Best season.** Front beaches are excellent November through April. Ocean beaches are patrolled summer weekends and school holidays; outside that window, only experienced swimmers and surfers should enter the water. Walks are best outside the heat of summer, the Two Bays Walk is exposed.

**What to bring.** Water (always, especially on the Two Bays Walk, no taps). A printed map for Greens Bush, phone reception is unreliable. Sun protection. A rash top for snorkelling at Mushroom Reef or Rye Pier.

## Frequently asked questions

**Which beach is best for kids?**
Mothers Beach in Mornington, sheltered by the pier, shallow, patrolled on select summer days, close to cafes and playgrounds. Safety Beach, Rye Front and Rosebud are also consistently calm. Avoid Bass Strait back beaches for young children.

**Where can I take my dog?**
Year-round off-leash: Tassells Cove (Safety Beach), Hawker Beach (Mount Martha), Fossil Beach (Mornington), Flinders Beach north end, Somers Beach (with time variations), Anthony's Nose (Dromana). Nowhere in the Mornington Peninsula National Park, every ocean back beach is included in that prohibition. Shire bay beaches allow on-leash dogs, but with a 9am–7pm sand prohibition during daylight saving.

**What's the difference between a front beach and a back beach?**
Front beaches face Port Phillip Bay, calm, shallow, close to the towns. Back beaches face Bass Strait, open ocean, surf, cliffs, strong rip currents. Front is for swimming and paddling; back is for surfing and cliff-top walks.

**Is the Two Bays Walk hard?**
Grade 3 moderate, doable in a long day for fit walkers, or split across two days with a night at Lightwood Creek. The track is 26km one-way from Dromana to Cape Schanck. Harder sections: the climb up Arthurs Seat and the final descent to Cape Schanck. Greens Bush in the middle is relatively flat. Carry all your water.

The single best move a Peninsula spa weekend can make is to cut the driving. Most visitors book a random Mornington hotel, then commute thirty to forty-five minutes each way to Alba or Peninsula Hot Springs. That is ninety minutes of lost relaxation per spa visit, multiplied across the trip.

Stay within fifteen minutes of the spa you are actually booking, and the weekend feels twice as calm.

Here are the accommodation pairings that actually work for each spa, and the combinations worth treating as proper weekends.

The hot springs country: Peninsula Hot Springs and Alba Thermal Springs

Both major hot springs sit in Fingal, within about fifteen minutes of each other. The best stays are on the Red Hill plateau (wine country, ten to twenty minutes north) or at the southern tip (Cape Schanck to Sorrento, ten to twenty minutes south-west). Avoid Mornington town itself for a pure spa weekend: it adds thirty-five minutes of driving each way and dilutes the ritual.

Peninsula Hot Springs Glamping: the onsite option

For serious bathers, the simplest stay-and-soak combination is Peninsula Hot Springs Glamping. Tented accommodation on the Peninsula Hot Springs property itself, with bathhouse access included. No drive. You finish the evening session and walk to your tent. The limitation: design is functional rather than luxurious, and the weather dependency is real in winter. For summer or shoulder-season bathers who want zero commute, this is the unmatched option.

Jackalope Hotel: the premium ridge stay

Jackalope Hotel in Merricks North is twenty minutes from both hot springs and the single most editorially coherent pairing on the Peninsula. Dark architecture, Subtle Energies treatments at Spa by Jackalope, and Doot Doot Doot’s two-hat restaurant on-property. This is the weekend to book for an anniversary, a birthday, or a first serious Peninsula couples trip. Pair a Jackalope spa morning with an Alba afternoon session and you have one of the country’s best wellness weekends.

Lindenderry Country House: the winery stay

Lindenderry at Red Hill sits on one of the Peninsula’s most established wine estates and is fifteen to twenty minutes from both hot springs. The building is English-country-estate in style rather than design-hotel, which suits a different traveller: quieter, more classical, with a good onsite restaurant and tennis courts for non-spa partners. Excellent for two-to-four-night stays.

Hotel Sorrento: the village alternative

Hotel Sorrento is twenty-five minutes from the hot springs but puts you in the centre of Sorrento village, which solves the dining and non-spa hours of the weekend. For mixed couples where one partner wants bathing and the other wants ocean walks and long lunches, Hotel Sorrento is the better base than a ridge hotel.
