If a flight is cancelled due to weather, the operator offers a reschedule for the next available flying day, which may be several days away. Refund policies for weather cancellations should be confirmed at the time of booking, as terms vary. Book as early in your Peninsula stay as possible to allow time for a reschedule if needed. The champagne breakfast venue is arranged by the operator and is typically a local winery; guests do not need to make separate reservations.
Flights cancelled due to weather are offered a reschedule to the next available flying day; refund terms are outlined at booking.
How early is the start time, and how does the morning work?

In summer, sunrise is earlier but conditions can require a slightly later launch. The operator confirms the exact pick-up or meet time with guests the evening before. The total morning including ground assembly, the flight, and the champagne breakfast runs approximately 4 hours, so guests are typically back at their accommodation by 9:30 to 10:30am.
What happens if the weather cancels the flight?

If conditions are unsafe, the operator contacts guests by phone or text the evening before or the morning of the flight. Cancelled flights are offered a reschedule to the next available flying day, which may be 2 to 5 days later depending on the forecast. If you cannot reschedule within your stay, the operator's refund policy applies: confirm the exact terms when booking, as they are updated periodically. To maximise your chances of flying, book as early in your Peninsula stay as possible so there is time to reschedule.
What is included in the champagne breakfast, and where does it take place?

The champagne breakfast follows the flight and is arranged by the operator at a winery or similar venue in the Red Hill or Merricks area. Private pickup from Melbourne CBD or a nominated hotel. The Moonlit Sanctuary Twilight Tour is a guided nocturnal walk through the park after dark, timed to coincide with when the resident Australian native animals are most active. The small group is led by a guide who handles and presents animals including eastern quolls, bettongs, brush-tailed phascogales, and little penguins, providing conservation context throughout. Tour sizes are capped at 20 participants to maintain a close, quiet experience.

Participants meet at the park entrance at the designated tour time, which varies by season to align with local sunset. The guide leads the group through enclosures and nocturnal habitat zones in sequence, pausing at each animal station for presentations and close-up encounters. Several species can be handled or approached at very close range under guide supervision, including threatened species that visitors rarely encounter in the wild or in larger zoo settings. The quoll and phascogale presentations are genuinely rare anywhere in Victoria. The guide provides information on the park's captive breeding programmes and the conservation threats facing each species. The walk is conducted at an easy pace on gravel and paved paths, mostly outdoors, and covers the full circuit of the park. Total tour duration is approximately 90 minutes.

Families with children aged 4 and above who want an educational wildlife experience rather than a passive zoo visit. International visitors for whom Australian nocturnal species are genuinely unfamiliar. School groups seeking curriculum-relevant conservation content. Adults with a serious interest in Australian wildlife and conservation who want access to species they are unlikely to encounter elsewhere in Victoria.

Guests expecting a large, varied zoo experience with dozens of species: the sanctuary is intimate and the species list is focused on threatened natives. Visitors who prefer to explore independently without a guide. Groups wanting something high-energy or sensory: the tour is deliberately quiet and calm to avoid disturbing the animals.

The Twilight Tour runs on specific evenings, not every night. Before booking, check the online calendar carefully, as dates are scheduled in advance and vary by season. School holiday periods, particularly summer and Easter, book out weeks ahead, and this is not an experience where you can rely on turning up and getting a spot. The tour is mostly outdoors on paved and gravel paths, so bring a light jacket even in summer as park temperatures drop after dark. Parking is available on-site. The park is a self-drive destination with no public transport connections, located approximately 45 minutes from central Melbourne via the Peninsula Link.
Bookings are required in advance; cancellation policies are outlined at the time of booking on the operator's website.
What animals will we see on the Twilight Tour?

The animal line-up varies by season and availability, but typically includes eastern quolls, bettongs, brush-tailed phascogales, little penguins, koalas, and a range of other Australian native species. Eastern quolls and brush-tailed phascogales are highlights that are genuinely rare to encounter anywhere else in Victoria. The guide confirms which animals are active on the night at the start of the tour.
What age is the tour suitable for?

The tour is suitable for children aged 4 and above. Younger children may find the pace and the after-dark setting challenging. Children under 16 must be accompanied by a paying adult. The tour involves some walking on outdoor paths after dark, so participants should be comfortable with that environment. The sanctuary recommends the twilight experience over daytime entry for families, as the animals are considerably more active after dark.
Is the tour indoors or outdoors, and what should we wear?

The Twilight Tour is predominantly outdoors, moving between outdoor enclosures and habitat zones on paved and gravel paths. The sanctuary is partially shaded, and temperatures drop noticeably after sunset even in warmer months. Bring a light jacket or layer, closed-toe shoes suitable for walking on uneven ground, and insect repellent. Torchlight is provided by the guide, so personal torches are optional but useful.

Moonraker's whale watching tour runs from June through October, when humpback and southern right whales migrate through Port Phillip Heads on their way along the Victorian coastline. The tour operates from Sorrento Pier on a vessel accommodating up to 36 passengers, with all viewing from the deck rather than in the water. Outside the whale season, the same tour departs as a dolphin and bay wildlife cruise.

Departure is from Sorrento Pier, with the vessel heading toward Port Phillip Heads and the open waters of Bass Strait where whale activity is concentrated during the June to October season. The crew monitors sighting reports and uses knowledge of whale movement corridors to position the vessel. Viewing is from the deck throughout: there is no in-water component. The naturalist guide provides commentary on species identification, whale behaviour, and the biology of the migration route. When whales are present, the vessel observes the minimum approach distances required under Victorian marine wildlife regulations. On tours where whales are not encountered, or outside the June to October season, the cruise continues as a dolphin and bay wildlife tour with commentary on the Port Phillip Bay marine environment. Total time on the water is approximately 2.5 to 3 hours.

Families with children of any age, mixed groups where some members cannot or do not want to enter the water, and guests with limited mobility who want a marine wildlife experience from a stable vessel platform. Anyone visiting the Peninsula between June and October who wants a reasonable chance of seeing humpback or southern right whales without an active water experience.

Guests who specifically want an in-water wildlife encounter: this tour is observation from the deck only. Anyone booking with whale sightings as a fixed expectation outside the June to October season will be disappointed, as sightings are rare in other months. Groups of fewer than 10 who want an intimate, private feel may find the 36-person capacity tour feels crowded when full.

The whale watching season runs from June through October. Bookings within this window offer genuine sighting prospects, with humpbacks typically more common in June to August and southern rights more likely in August to October, though overlap is common. Outside this window, the tour operates as a dolphin and bay wildlife cruise: this is still a worthwhile outing, but it is not a whale watching experience. The operator's sighting guarantee policy varies, so check the current terms on the booking page before committing. Booking a week or more in advance is advisable in July and August, when the season peak coincides with school holidays. Bring layers: the bay can be cold and windy even on clear days, particularly near the Heads.
Cancellations due to unsafe weather or sea conditions are managed by the operator, typically with a reschedule or credit.
When are whales most reliably seen on this tour?

The whale watching season runs from June through October, when humpback and southern right whales migrate along the Victorian coast through Port Phillip Heads. Sighting rates are highest in July, August, and September. Outside this window, whale encounters are rare and the tour operates as a dolphin and bay wildlife cruise instead.
What happens if no whales are spotted?

Whale sightings cannot be guaranteed on any individual tour, even within the season. The operator's current policy on refunds or rebooking for no-sighting tours is detailed on the booking page and should be checked before purchase, as terms are updated periodically. Within the season, the crew will redirect to dolphin and bay wildlife activity if whales are not found. Outside the season, the tour is listed and sold as a dolphin cruise, not a whale watch.
Is there a minimum age for children, and is the tour suitable for young families?

There is no stated minimum age, and the vessel is a larger, more stable platform than a RIB-based tour, which makes it more manageable for young children and guests with mobility concerns. Seas near Port Phillip Heads can be rougher than the inner Bay, particularly in winter, so guests prone to motion sickness should be prepared. The deck is open, so dress children in warm, windproof layers regardless of the season.

Polperro's dolphin swim tour puts participants in the water alongside wild bottlenose dolphins in Port Phillip Bay, departing from Sorrento Pier in groups of up to 12. Encounters are guided by licensed marine naturalists who position swimmers near dolphin pods while the RIB holds station nearby. The tour runs year-round, though summer and autumn offer the warmest water temperatures.

After a briefing at the pier covering safety, marine mammal interaction rules, and what to expect in the water, the group boards the rigid inflatable boat and heads out into Port Phillip Bay. The crew uses knowledge of regular dolphin movement patterns to locate pods, typically within 20 to 30 minutes of departure. When a pod is found and conditions allow safe entry, swimmers enter the water with snorkel, mask, and wetsuit (provided). Dolphins are not baited or directed, so interaction depends on the animals' interest, but pods in the Bay are habituated to the vessel and frequently approach curious swimmers. Non-swimmers and younger observers (children under 8) can remain on board and watch from the vessel. After the swim session, the boat may relocate to a second pod before returning to the pier. Total time on the water is approximately 2.5 to 3 hours.

Families with children aged 8 and above who want a genuine, unscripted wildlife encounter rather than a themed attraction. Confident swimmers who are comfortable in open water with a snorkel. Guests who understand that wild dolphin encounters are not guaranteed but who appreciate the difference between a managed interaction and a zoo-style experience. Suitable for adults travelling without children who want a close-up wildlife experience in a small group.

Families with children under 8 who specifically want to swim, as the minimum swim age is 8 years old (younger children may observe from the vessel, but cannot enter the water). Guests who are not comfortable in cold, open water: Port Phillip Bay temperatures sit around 13 to 16 degrees Celsius in winter and spring, and up to 22 degrees in peak summer, and wetsuits are provided but the cold is real. Anyone seeking a passive, seated sightseeing experience rather than active participation.

Tours operate year-round with multiple departures daily in peak season. Summer and autumn offer the most comfortable water temperatures and the highest dolphin activity near the pier. Book at least a week in advance in December through February, when tours fill quickly. The operator provides wetsuits, masks, and snorkels, so participants need only bring a towel, sunscreen, and a change of clothes. Arrive at Sorrento Pier at least 15 minutes before the scheduled departure for the shore briefing. Cancellations due to weather or unsafe marine conditions are managed by the operator and typically result in a reschedule or full refund.

The minimum age to enter the water is 8 years old. Children under 8 are welcome on board the vessel and can watch encounters from the RIB, but cannot participate in the swim. Adults accompanying non-swimming children will also remain on the vessel during in-water sessions unless another adult is present to supervise the child on board.

Dolphin sightings are not guaranteed on any individual tour. If no dolphins are encountered, the operator's policy is to offer a complimentary re-booking rather than a cash refund. Check the current policy on the booking page, as terms can be updated seasonally.

Bring a towel, a change of clothes, sunscreen, and any motion sickness medication if you are prone to it on small vessels. Leave valuables at your accommodation or in a locker at the pier if available. The RIB is an open boat with no cabin, so dress for outdoor conditions on the day.

Yes. Rick's Wine Tours operates exclusively as a private charter. You will not share the vehicle with guests from other bookings. Groups of 2–24 are accommodated; confirm your group size and vehicle type with the operator at booking.
Are cellar door tasting fees included in the price?

This is not confirmed in the published fare and should be verified directly with the operator before booking. It is a material cost difference from competitors who include tastings — confirm in writing whether tasting fees are bundled or payable separately at each stop.
How flexible is the itinerary really?

Meaningful flexibility requires advance planning, not on-the-day decision-making. Each winery stop needs to be pre-arranged against the venue's booking schedule and seasonal closures. The earlier preferences are communicated, the more the operator can lock in the preferred itinerary. Treat itinerary planning as a conversation before the day, not an option during it.

The 40-minute roll-on/roll-off ferry crossing between Sorrento and Queenscliff traverses Port Phillip Bay and connects the Mornington Peninsula to the Bellarine Peninsula. For adults, it is a practical route that bypasses the Melbourne ring-road. For children, it tends to become the most memorable part of the day.

The ferry departs Sorrento Terminal on the Mornington Peninsula foreshore, crosses Port Phillip Bay, and arrives at Queenscliff on the Bellarine Peninsula. The crossing takes approximately 40 minutes. The vessel has a car deck for roll-on/roll-off vehicle transport, a passenger saloon, and open upper decks. Foot passengers and cyclists travel at a lower fare and can board without vehicle booking. Multiple sailings depart daily from both terminals; the schedule varies by season. Queenscliff offers heritage buildings, marine precinct, coffee, and the start of the Great Ocean Road corridor for those continuing south.

Families with children who want the bay crossing to feel like an event rather than a drive. The crossing removes the Melbourne ring-road entirely for guests based in Sorrento and wanting to reach the Bellarine Peninsula. Day trippers doing a return crossing get a genuine narrative structure to their Saturday: you went somewhere, arrived somewhere else, and came back by boat.

Travellers in a hurry — the crossing adds 40 minutes each way plus terminal time. Guests who need to bring a vehicle in peak season without advance booking: vehicle spots fill on busy weekends and the car deck requires pre-booking. Anyone prone to seasickness: the bay is sheltered but small swell is normal.

Foot passengers can board on the day without booking — turn up at the terminal and purchase tickets. Vehicle bookings are strongly recommended on weekends and school holidays, particularly for the 10am–2pm sailings. Ticket prices are per passenger plus a vehicle surcharge if applicable. Confirm current timetables at searoad.com.au before building your day around a specific sailing. Storm cancellations are rare; Searoad has high operational reliability year-round.
Tickets are flexible and transferable. Storm cancellations notified directly and rescheduling options available.
Do I need to book the ferry in advance?

Foot passengers do not need to book — you can purchase tickets at the terminal. Vehicle bookings are recommended on weekends and school holidays. Check searoad.com.au for the current timetable and to pre-book vehicle passage.
What is there to do in Queenscliff on a day crossing?

Queenscliff has a heritage main street, several good cafes, the Queenscliff–Portarlington ferry connection, and the start of the Bellarine Rail Trail for cyclists. The Marine Discovery Centre is 2 minutes from the ferry terminal. For families, a 2–3 hour Queenscliff layover is usually enough before the return crossing.
Can you do a return crossing as a foot passenger in one day?

Yes. A return foot-passenger crossing fits comfortably into a family day based in Sorrento. Take an 8:30am or 9:30am sailing to Queenscliff, spend 2–3 hours exploring, and return on a midday or early afternoon sailing. The full day still leaves time for a beach stop or snorkel tour in Portsea.
What if the ferry is cancelled?

Searoad operates year-round with high reliability. Cancellations due to storm conditions are rare and communicated in advance. Tickets are flexible — reschedule or seek a refund directly with Searoad.

Temptation Sailing's bay cruise departs Sorrento Pier aboard a classic sailing vessel for a half-day passage across Port Phillip Bay. The pace is deliberately unhurried: sailing is the primary experience, with wildlife encounters a welcome possibility rather than the focus. Dolphin sightings are common but not structured into the itinerary. Groups are capped at 18 to keep the vessel uncrowded.

After boarding at Sorrento Pier, the skipper sets sail into Port Phillip Bay with the course varying according to wind conditions on the day. The journey out into the open bay typically takes 30 to 45 minutes before the vessel settles into its main sailing passage. Guests can move around the deck, talk with the skipper about the vessel and the Bay, and take turns at the helm if they are interested. Dolphin pods are frequently encountered in the shipping lanes and near the Heads: when this happens, the skipper adjusts course for a closer look without disrupting the animals. The return leg brings the vessel back to Sorrento with a different heading, often with the Mornington Peninsula hills visible to the east. Total time on the water is approximately 3 to 3.5 hours. Sunset sail departures are available on selected dates and offer a different character to the morning cruise.

Couples looking for a relaxed, genuinely scenic outing that is not structured around ticking off sights. Adults with an interest in sailing, seamanship, or the bay's geography and ecology. Small groups (4 to 10 people) who want something more personal than a commercial wildlife charter. Suitable for anniversary occasions where the point is the experience of being on the water together rather than a specific activity.

Families with children under 5: the open sailing vessel environment, length of time underway, and lack of child-specific programming make this a poor fit for very young children. Guests primarily seeking a guaranteed, close-range wildlife encounter should book with Polperro Dolphin Swims, which is purpose-built for that outcome. Guests who are prone to motion sickness should be aware that Port Phillip Bay swell is variable and the vessel is under sail, not power, so motion cannot be entirely controlled.

The bay cruise is available as a shared-boat booking (up to 18 guests total) or as a private charter. For anniversary occasions or private groups, the charter option is worth the premium: it allows custom departure times and removes the variable of other guests. Shared departures tend to have a consistent mix of couples and small groups. Booking a week in advance is generally sufficient outside peak summer; in December and January and on long weekends, two weeks is more reliable. The skipper will communicate any weather-related changes the evening before departure. Light layers are recommended regardless of season, as the bay breeze is cooler than onshore temperatures suggest.
Weather-related cancellations are communicated in advance by the operator, with reschedule or refund options provided.
Do I need any sailing experience to join the cruise?

No prior sailing experience is needed. The vessel is skippered throughout and guests are passengers, not crew. Anyone who wants to learn more about the boat or have a turn at the helm is welcome to ask the skipper, but there is no expectation of participation beyond being present on deck. The experience is designed to be accessible to guests who have never sailed before.
What happens if the weather is bad on the day?

The skipper assesses conditions before each departure and will contact guests if the tour needs to be cancelled or modified due to unsafe weather. Port Phillip Bay is a protected body of water and many days that look overcast or windy on land are perfectly sailable. If the departure is cancelled by the operator, guests are offered a reschedule or a full refund. Guests who cancel themselves within a short window of departure may be subject to the operator's standard cancellation terms, so check the booking conditions at time of purchase.
Can we bring food and drinks on board?

Check directly with Temptation Sailing on their current BYO policy, as this can vary by vessel and by booking type. In general, many smaller sailing operators in Victoria permit guests to bring their own food and non-alcoholic drinks, and some permit BYO wine for private charters. The operator can advise at the time of booking what is permitted and whether any catering add-ons are available.

Wine Hop and Coastal Tours holds an Ecotourism Australia certification, which distinguishes it from the broader Peninsula wine tour field. The day combines structured coastal interpretation at Peninsula sites with cellar door tastings and an included lunch, and operates on Fridays only.

Pickup from Melbourne CBD hotels in the morning, followed by a nine-hour day that sequences coastal stops with cellar door visits. The guide's coastal interpretation is substantive: the Ecotourism Australia accreditation requires documented standards for environmental commentary, not just scenic stops. Lunch is included at a Peninsula winery. Two cellar door tastings are incorporated around the coastal segments. The Friday-only schedule means coastal sites are typically less crowded than on weekend departures. Return to Melbourne CBD hotels in the late afternoon, with Friday peak-hour traffic a factor on the return leg.

Guests who want the Peninsula's coastal character as the centrepiece of the day, not just a break between cellar doors. Those with a genuine interest in coastal ecology and environmental interpretation. Guests who can take a Friday and prefer the lighter crowds that the weekday schedule delivers.

Anyone who cannot take a Friday: this is the single structurally limiting factor for this tour. Guests who want to compare operators on Tripadvisor volume: the 18-review sample is too small to draw confident conclusions, and the 3.7 average warrants reading the individual reviews before booking.

Friday-only operation creates real booking friction — confirm your specific departure date is available before making travel plans. Cancellation policy is: full refund with more than 48 hours notice (less a credit card processing fee); no refund inside 48 hours or for no-shows. Allow for Friday afternoon traffic on the return to Melbourne when planning post-tour commitments.
Full refund with more than 48 hours notice, less a credit card processing fee. No refund for cancellations inside 48 hours or no-shows.
What does the Ecotourism Australia certification mean in practice?

Ecotourism Australia's National Ecotourism Accreditation Program requires operators to meet documented standards in environmental management, interpretation quality, and contribution to conservation. For the guest, it means the guide's commentary on coastal environments is structured and accurate rather than improvised, and the tour avoids practices that cause ecological harm at sensitive sites.
Why does this tour only run on Fridays?

The Friday-only schedule reflects the capacity constraints of a small-group specialist operation. The practical upside: Peninsula coastal sites on a Friday are materially less crowded than on weekends. If a Friday departure works for your schedule, the timing is an advantage.
Yes. The operator's booking page references an included lunch as part of the tour. Communicate dietary requirements at the time of booking, as the midday stop is the day's key fixed inclusion.

The Peninsula's second-generation thermal springs complex  -  cleaner architecture, smaller crowds, better pacing than the original

Alba is the thermal springs the Peninsula had been waiting for. Where Peninsula Hot Springs has become a must-photograph theme park, Alba opened in 2022 with a deliberately stripped-back approach: thirty-one geothermal pools set into a quiet landscape in Fingal, a better spa building, and a ticketing system that caps bather numbers so the experience doesn't collapse into chaos.

The architecture is confident without being showy. The hot and cold circuits are properly sequenced. The on-site cafe is sensible. And the whole thing feels more like a European bath day than a tourist attraction  -  which is exactly what most Peninsula visitors want and rarely get from the category.

Book a morning session. Do the full thermal circuit properly rather than hopping. Lunch on the ridge afterwards and you have one of the most complete days the Peninsula offers.

Ashcombe Maze is the Peninsula's most unexpectedly charming detour. Shashi and Rohit Singh's biodynamic family estate  -  home to one of the Peninsula's only serious Syrah programs alongside Amrit single-vineyard Pinot

Avani is the Peninsula's quiet Syrah specialist, and that alone is reason to visit. Shashi and Rohit Singh run the estate as a genuinely small family operation  -  biodynamically farmed, hand-worked, and unusually focused on Syrah at a time when nearly every other cellar door on the ridge has all-in on Pinot Noir. Avani was Gourmet Traveller's Best Small Cellar Door (Mornington) in 2023 and it earned every word of the citation.

Book ahead. Ask for the skin-contact. Bring home a bottle of the Syrah  -  it ages quietly and well.

This is not a destination Japanese in the Melbourne sense. It is a solid neighbourhood option with a handful of seats at a small sushi counter, and a clear purpose in a town where the dining scene leans heavily toward pasta, pizza, and Peninsula wine restaurants. Barmah Park has quietly turned itself into the Peninsula's most serious cellar-door-as-dining-experience. The signature tasting is a structured five-wine, five-canape pairing run out of a small kitchen that cooks like a hatted restaurant: one canape designed for each wine, paced and explained, across a single relaxed hour at a communal wooden table. The wines are quietly excellent  -  Italian-leaning varieties alongside the Peninsula standards  -  but the real draw is the format. Eldridge is where Peninsula Pinot nerds go to geek out. David Lloyd runs the estate almost single-handedly, makes the wine himself, and produces single-clone bottlings  -  MV6, PTG, 115, 777  -  in quantities so small that most of them are sold out by word of mouth before they reach a shelf. The Baillieu family's 1972 vineyard  -  the planting that started the modern Peninsula wine region

Elgee Park is where the modern Mornington Peninsula wine industry actually began. Baillie Baillieu planted vines here in 1972, three years before Main Ridge Estate, at a time when Victoria's cool-climate wine region had yet to exist as a concept. The estate is still in family hands, the plantings still trace the original blocks, and the wines  -  Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, and a quietly exceptional Viognier  -  carry the kind of restraint only decades of the same family farming the same soil can produce.

The cellar door is low-key, rural, and unhurried. There is no restaurant, no sculpture walk, no attempt to turn the visit into a day-trip set piece. You taste, you talk, and you leave understanding a little more about how the Peninsula wine region actually came to be. The Viognier is a surprise  -  barely anyone on the Peninsula still plants the variety, and Elgee Park has been making good ones for thirty years.

Open limited days  -  check ahead. Bring a genuine interest in Peninsula wine history; you will be rewarded.

For anniversary weekends staying at a Mornington bayside hotel, a couples treatment here is the simplest wellness move — no drive, no parking issue, no restaurant time lost.

Families are welcome, groups are easy, and the whole place runs at the friendly mid-volume that makes a weeknight visit as enjoyable as a Saturday.

Use it as your bayside brewery default. Closer to the beach than the hinterland breweries and the easiest one to drop into mid-day.

Johnny Ripe is the pie stop the Peninsula has needed for years, and the one visitors end up returning to on every subsequent trip. Kooyong is the Peninsula's most consistently serious producer of single-vineyard wine, and the cellar door reflects it. Planted in 1975 by Nat and Rosalie White — the Peninsula's founding vineyard, still making restrained Pinot and Chardonnay from the original blocks

Main Ridge Estate is the vineyard that started it all. Nat and Rosalie White planted the first vines up here in 1975 when nobody in Victoria quite believed cool-climate Pinot could be taken seriously, and the property remains a pilgrimage for anyone who cares about how the Peninsula wine region actually came to exist. The cellar door is small, the tasting room sits in a quiet bush setting on top of the ridge, and the wines  -  Chardonnay from the Half Acre and Three Quarter Acre blocks, Pinot Noir from the Half Acre  -  still hold to the restrained, structured, long-lived style the Whites established four decades ago.

The kitchen runs a short lunch menu Friday through Sunday, built around the wines rather than competing with them. There is no attempt to turn the place into a wedding venue or sculpture park; this is a working estate where the founders are still quietly in residence and the wines are bottled under Tim Shand's exacting hand.

Go mid-week in winter if you want the quietest tasting. Order the Half Acre Pinot with a cheese plate and an hour to yourself.

A small, long-standing estate with one of the Peninsula's rare serious Shiraz programs and a windswept coastal vineyard

Merricks Estate is one of those Peninsula cellar doors that has resisted all temptation to grow. George and Jacky Kefford planted the estate in 1977 on a windswept block close to Western Port  -  one of the coolest, most exposed positions in the region  -  and the estate is still small, still family-run, and still committed to the same short line-up of wines: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, and, unusually for the Peninsula, a serious Shiraz.

The Shiraz is the conversation piece. Only a handful of Peninsula producers take the variety seriously; Merricks Estate has done so for four decades and the bottlings are distinctive  -  peppery, cool-climate, closer in spirit to the northern Rhône than to the Barossa. The tasting room is quiet and unvarnished, the pour is generous, and the whole visit feels like stepping slightly off the main cellar-door circuit.

Go on a weekday for the quietest experience. Buy a bottle of the Shiraz. Drink it with winter lamb.

Merricks General Wine Store occupies what used to be the village's original general store and it has turned that bones into one of the most likeable rooms on the Peninsula. Richard McIntyre's pioneering low-intervention estate — home to the Robinson Chardonnay, one of Australia's genuine Chardonnay reference points

Moorooduc Estate is one of the quietest landmarks in Australian wine. Richard McIntyre has been making wine here for more than thirty years and is genuinely one of the country's elder statesmen of low-intervention, wild-yeast winemaking. The Robinson Chardonnay  -  made from a single block, wild-fermented, aged in old French oak  -  is a reference point for what Peninsula Chardonnay can be at the very top of its game.

The cellar door is open on weekends and for booked visits during the week. It is not a destination experience in the modern sense: no sculpture trail, no vineyard accommodation, no restaurant. It is a tasting room at a working winery where the winemaker himself is often in the room. Go when you want to understand what serious Chardonnay tastes like before anyone started chasing fashion.

Ask to taste the Robinson and the Garden Pinot back-to-back. Buy the Robinson. Decant it before you pour it.

A tiny Flinders estate with natural-fermented wines and guest accommodation inside reconverted 1930s railway carriages

Nazaaray is one of the true eccentrics of the Peninsula wine scene, and that is the entire point. The estate is tiny, the owners are hands-on, the wines are naturally fermented with wild yeast, and the guesthouses on site are made from reconverted 1930s train carriages  -  the kind of one-of-one experience you cannot contrive in a marketing brief.

The wines are genuinely idiosyncratic. They will not taste like the Peninsula average; they will taste like whatever the vintage, the wild yeast, and the owners' instincts decided they would be in any given year. For anyone who finds the ridge cellar doors starting to blur together, Nazaaray is the reset.

Call ahead. Tasting hours are limited and the welcome is personal. Stay the night in one of the train carriages if you can  -  there are only a few on the Peninsula wine circuit that do accommodation, and none of them do it quite like this.

Mike Aylward's precise, minimal cellar door turning out some of the Peninsula's most quietly obsessive pinot noir

Ocean Eight is the kind of cellar door that wine people send other wine people to and casual tasters sometimes overlook. That's a mistake. Mike Aylward grew up in Peninsula wine country  -  his family founded Kooyong  -  and Ocean Eight was the project he built when he decided he wanted to do something smaller, quieter, and more single-minded than the big names allow.

The Verve and Aylward Pinot Noirs are among the most structured and ageable wines being made on the Peninsula. The chardonnay holds its own against the region's benchmarks. The tasting room is minimal and unpretentious: you sit down, the wines come out, and Mike or one of the family walks you through them without any of the theatre that creeps into larger cellar doors.

Book ahead  -  they keep numbers deliberately small. This is a tasting for people who want to understand why the Peninsula matters.

Onannon is the kind of Peninsula producer you find on the lists of the best restaurants in Melbourne and Sydney long before you find it at the supermarket. Three winemakers  -  Will Byron, Kaspar Hermann and Sam Middleton  -  formed the project years ago to make tiny batches of restrained, elegant Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and the wines have become quiet cult favourites among the people who drink for a living.

The style is deliberate: low-intervention, minimal oak, acid-driven, built for the table rather than the trophy cabinet. The Main Ridge Pinot is the headline. The Foothills Chardonnay is the winemaker's pick.

Cellar door visits are limited and by appointment  -  this is a small project with day-jobs attached  -  so check the website for current availability. Go when you can. Buy a couple of bottles. You'll want them on a winter Sunday.

For non-resort guests it is a bookable day-spa experience. For resort guests it is the anchor of a serious wellness stay.

Peninsula Hot Springs has been open since 2005 and in that time it has grown from a few pools in a paddock into the most ambitious wellness complex in the country. Book the Bath House premium session midweek if you can, or a Twilight session in the cooler months. The Hilltop Pool, the Reflexology Walk, and the private baths reward people who actually move through the circuit properly rather than photographing it.

Pier Street Fresh Seafood is the Peninsula fish-and-chips ritual in one address. Red Hill Brewery is the oldest serious craft brewery on the Peninsula and still one of the few in Australia that grows its own hops. That detail matters: the farm-to-glass story here is not marketing, it is infrastructure. Dave and Karen Golding planted the hop garden in 2005 and have been making Belgian-style ales from it ever since  -  witbier, dubbel, tripel, and the seasonal fresh-hop beers that are worth waiting for.

The cellar door is a low barn at the top of a vineyard track, with picnic tables, a wood-fired pizza oven, and a tasting flight that doubles as a civilised lunch. Bring the dog. Bring walking shoes for the hop garden loop afterwards.

A proper alternative to a winery lunch if your group includes someone who actively dislikes pinot noir.

Small-batch cheesemaker with a tasting room  -  hard sheep's milk styles, washed rinds, and a rotating seasonal list

Red Hill Cheese is one of the Peninsula's quietest food landmarks. The tasting room is small and the range is deliberately tight: hard sheep's milk styles, a washed rind or two, a rotating seasonal list of whatever the cheesemaker is currently excited about. The pours are generous enough to understand what is happening on the plate, and the team is happy to talk through milk sourcing, ageing, and why a Peninsula block grows cheese the way it does.

Buy a wedge on the way out. Pair it with a loaf from Red Hill Bakery and a bottle from one of the estates down the road, and you have lunch sorted for a quiet afternoon at a holiday house.

Not a destination in its own right, but an essential stop on any serious Peninsula food weekend.

Red Hill Estate has one of the most arresting cellar-door positions on the Peninsula  -  the slope falls away toward Western Port, French Island sits in the middle distance, and on clear days Phillip Island comes into view at the horizon. It is one of those rare Peninsula vineyards where the geography does most of the sales work before you even open a bottle.

The traditional-method sparkling program is quietly one of the Peninsula's best: the Blanc de Blancs rewards the drive, and the rosé is a year-round favourite at the estate tables. Worth pairing with lunch elsewhere on the ridge before or after tasting through the cellar door.

Red Hill Recreation Reserve, 172 Arthurs Seat Rd, Red Hill VIC 3937
Victoria's finest artisan craft market, held the first Saturday of each month  -  more than 200 stalls of craft, produce, plants and peninsular makers

Red Hill Market is the single monthly event that pulls the whole Peninsula together. Held on the first Saturday of each month from September through May, the market spreads across the Red Hill Recreation Reserve with more than 200 stalls of handmade craft, gourmet produce, plants, artisan food, and the kind of small-run peninsular makers who do not have retail shops anywhere else.

The market is big, unapologetically so, and the best way to experience it is to commit to the full morning. Arrive by 9am for parking, work through the food stalls first, circle back for the plants and the craft, and leave before the late-morning crush kicks in. Coffee from one of the mobile roasters; a breakfast sandwich from the Balnarring Bakehouse stall; honey from a ridge apiarist; a bunch of ranunculus from the Merricks flower grower.

One of the Peninsula's essential weekend experiences. Plan a whole weekend around it if you can  -  the cellar doors are quieter after midday, and the market sets the mood for the rest of the day.

Peninsula truffière running seasonal truffle hunts with trained dogs  -  a morning in the field, a cellar-door tasting, and fresh truffles for sale when in season

Red Hill Truffles is a working truffière on the ridge that opens for seasonal truffle hunts from late autumn through winter. The format is the one every winter food-obsessive on the Peninsula eventually books: a morning in the field with the trained dogs, watching them work each row and nose out the black truffle hidden under the inoculated oaks, followed by a small tasting back at the shed where the truffles go into eggs, butter, and whatever the kitchen is running that week.

Truffle seasons are short and the weekend slots book out early every year. Go in June or July if you can, dress warmly, and understand that the point is the process  -  the hunt itself  -  as much as the truffle on the plate. Fresh truffles are available for sale when they are up.

One of the Peninsula's most unusual winter experiences. Book months in advance for weekends.

An enormous foreshore pub a short walk from Rye's front beach  -  family-friendly, deck-oriented, and the right answer on a warm afternoon

The Rye Hotel is enormous in the best possible sense  -  a sprawling foreshore pub that absorbs families, locals, and long weekend crowds without anybody noticing the place has filled up. The main deck catches the afternoon sun, the kids' menu is honest, and the kitchen does the straightforward things well enough that nobody complains. The beer garden fills on a hot Sunday; the bar absorbs the overflow.

This is not a fine-dining destination and nobody involved is pretending otherwise. The point is the position  -  a short walk from the front beach, a deck with enough shade, and a menu that lets the kids eat something they recognise while you work through a schooner and look at the bay.

Good for the broad, low-key kind of Peninsula afternoon that has nothing to prove.

The Sanctuary at Alba solves the problem that Peninsula Hot Springs never quite did: until June 2025, staying near the hot springs still meant leaving the springs to sleep. Paul Scorpo's tightly focused family estate making some of the Peninsula's most acclaimed Pinot Gris alongside elegant Chardonnay and Pinot Noir

Scorpo is a landscape architect's vineyard, and it shows. Paul Scorpo planted the estate in 1997 on a gently sloping block between Merricks and Dromana, designed the layout himself, and has spent the years since building one of the most tightly focused family wine operations on the Peninsula. The range is small  -  Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Rosé  -  and each of those bottles is taken unusually seriously.

The Pinot Gris is widely regarded as one of the best in the country: textural, phenolic, aged on lees long enough to carry real depth. The Estate Pinot Noir and the Bestia Chardonnay are the two bottles other Peninsula winemakers mention when asked what they drink at home.

Cellar door visits are by appointment. This is not a drop-in cellar door; it is a proper tasting-room experience for people who already know what they like and want to go deeper.

An Ocean Beach Road institution that has fed generations of beachgoers  -  pies, pasties, custard scrolls and a proper sourdough loaf

Sorrento Bakery has been in the same spot on Ocean Beach Road long enough that nobody in the village remembers the town without it. Spa by Jackalope is not trying to compete on scale. It is a tight, design-forward boutique spa inside the Jackalope Hotel vineyard, built to serve hotel guests and day visitors with treatments that match the broader Jackalope editorial: considered, unhurried, and quietly uncompromising.

For day visitors without a hotel booking: treatments are available, but the property is designed for guests first. The better single-visit experience for non-stayers is One Spa at RACV Cape Schanck or Alba Thermal Springs.

Former horse-training stables turned sprawling brewery  -  wood-fired pizzas, Sunday roasts, acres of lawn, and the Peninsula's best brewery-day-out address

St Andrews Beach Brewery occupies the former stables of a racehorse training property, and the scale of the place is part of the experience. Acres of lawn roll out to the former exercise track; the brew house sits in the middle of the site; the kitchen runs wood-fired pizzas, loaded burgers, and a rotating roast on Sundays out of an open pass. Kids run between the tables, dogs run between the kids, and the whole operation has the feel of a country-estate afternoon that has accidentally turned into a brewery.

The beer is serious. The core range covers the Peninsula brewery-day hits  -  pale ale, lager, red ale, a session sour  -  and the rotating taps dip into more interesting territory when the brewers get ambitious. Paired with a wood-fired pizza and an afternoon on the lawn, it is the signature brewery stop on the Peninsula and the one that handles a group of twelve without blinking.

Book for Sunday lunch in summer. Arrive hungry. Bring a hat.

Stonier was planted in 1978 by Brian and Noel Stonier and remains one of the Peninsula's quietly essential producers. Some of the oldest Chardonnay and Pinot Noir vines on the Peninsula are on this property, and the wines they make  -  particularly the Reserve Chardonnay and the KBS Vineyard Pinot Noir  -  are textbook cool-climate Peninsula: precise, saline, structured, built to age.

The cellar door is grown-up rather than flashy. There is no wedding marquee, no sculpture trail, no all-day pizza kitchen. There is a tasting counter, a winemaker's-list flight that walks you through block-level thinking, and a small seasonal food offering if you time the visit properly. This is the Peninsula cellar door to recommend to the visitor who has been unimpressed by the louder venues on the ridge.

Ask for the Reserve flight. Take home a bottle of the KBS Pinot  -  it is one of the Peninsula's more age-worthy wines, and you'll want to drink it in five years, not tonight.

Sunny Ridge is the Peninsula's original pick-your-own strawberry farm and has been the default family day-out on the ridge for decades. The season runs roughly November through April, and the routine is the same every year: pick your own strawberries in the field, weigh them in at the counter, and reward the work with a strawberry ice cream or sundae from the farm café.

There is no pretending this is a sophisticated food experience, and it is not trying to be one. It is a working strawberry farm that has figured out how to do hospitality without losing its soul, and the kids will remember it long after they have forgotten whatever cellar door you dragged them to afterwards. The café does a perfectly respectable coffee and a lunch menu for the grown-ups while the children chase berries.

Go in the morning on a sunny day. Wear clothes you do not mind staining.

The Peninsula's Pinot Grigio pioneer — a sprawling, family-friendly winery cellar door with Italian-inspired food and the estate's Pinot Grigio by the glass

T'Gallant essentially invented Australian Pinot Grigio as a commercial category - Kathleen Quealy and Kevin McCarthy planted the first vines in the late 1980s and spent years convincing everyone else that Italian varieties belonged on the Peninsula. They went on to found Quealy; T'Gallant continued under the Treasury Wine Estates umbrella and is now the most reliably family-friendly cellar door on the Main Ridge.

The on-site dining has evolved from the old La Baracca trattoria format into a new menu concept — still Italian-inspired and designed for easy winery lunches, but updated. The tasting room is open daily, the flights move briskly, and the shaded outdoor area is still one of the best spots on the Plateau for a group lunch.

Come for the Pinot Grigio, stay for the food, and don't try to make it more than it is. T'Gallant is the Peninsula at its most unserious, and that is exactly its purpose.

Only Peninsula Winery Ageing in Terracotta Amphorae
The Peninsula's amphora winery  -  terracotta-aged wines, an Italian-leaning range, and a cellar that is worth the visit on its own

Trofeo Estate is the Peninsula's one and only amphora winery. The team ages a meaningful portion of the estate's production in terracotta pots rather than oak barrels, and the resulting wines  -  Sangiovese, Fiano, Nebbiolo  -  have a textural depth and a savoury edge that nothing else in the region produces. The ancient method sits oddly against the Peninsula's cool-climate reputation and that is exactly why it works.

The barrel room itself is worth the visit. Stepping into a Peninsula cellar and finding it lined with huge clay amphorae rather than the expected French oak is the kind of small shock that reorients how you think about the region's possibilities. The tasting is generous and the team is happy to explain the winemaking in genuine detail.

Book the cellar tour. Taste the Sangiovese and the Fiano back-to-back. Bring home whichever one most surprises you.

Tuck's Ridge is one of the Peninsula's longest-established estates  -  planted in the mid-1980s, repositioned under a refreshed team over the past few years, and quietly making some of the most interesting single-vineyard Pinot Noir on the ridge. The cellar door has been gently modernised without losing the country-estate feel, and the deck view  -  down across the vines toward Western Port  -  is the kind of thing that stops new visitors mid-sip.

The Turramurra Pinot Noir is the bottle to pay attention to, the Chardonnay rewards the rebuild, and the tasting program now includes small-format food pairings on weekends that lift the whole visit beyond a straight cellar-door stop.

Australia's first dedicated gluten-free brewery, unexpectedly good, and worth the drive to Dromana for the taproom alone.

Two Bays Brewing opened as Australia's first dedicated gluten-free brewery and has spent the years since quietly proving that the category does not have to taste like a compromise. The pale ale, lager, and session IPA are all genuinely good beers judged against any yardstick, and the taproom is the most welcoming destination on the Peninsula for anyone who has spent years sitting out the brewery tour.

The room is small and unfussy. Snacks are the brewery standards  -  pizzas, a burger, a charcuterie board  -  and the team pours with pride in what they are doing. For visitors with coeliac disease or a gluten sensitivity, this is the Peninsula's most inclusive beer stop; for everybody else, it is still worth the flight as an interesting comparison with the gluten-containing neighbours.

Check the website for current hours  -  Two Bays runs tighter than some of the bigger breweries.

A small warm Italian room tucked into the hinterland  -  handmade pasta, a short hand-written list, and the Peninsula's best neighbourhood trattoria

Via Boffe is the Peninsula trattoria that deserves much more attention than it gets. The room is small and warm  -  polished concrete, low lighting, an open kitchen that you can see from every seat  -  and the menu is a short hand-written list that changes with whatever the team feels like cooking that week. Handmade pasta is the headline, but the antipasti is where the kitchen really wakes up: fresh ricotta with olive oil and cracked pepper, grilled peaches with stracciatella, a wood-fired flatbread that disappears in three minutes.

This is the Peninsula version of the Italian room everyone wishes they had in their own suburb. The wine list leans into small Italian producers alongside a short Peninsula local shelf, and the team is genuinely happy to steer you toward something unexpected.

Book ahead  -  the room is tiny and it fills fast on weekends. Sit at the counter if you are a pair, order three pastas between you, and finish with the hazelnut torta.

Woodman Estate is the Peninsula's most distinctly pastoral villa option, and it is not trying to be a vineyard stay. The three standalone chalets are built directly over a private five-acre lake — 4-poster mahogany beds, marble bathrooms, double spa baths with lake views, gas open fires, private balconies. The 50-acre English country estate has formal gardens, natural bushland, a rowboat, tennis court, and billiards room. No vines, no cellar door — the argument is pastoral rather than wine-country, closer to the English country-house tradition than anything else on the Peninsula.

Jimmy Watson Memorial Trophy (2012 Block 1 Pinot Noir)
Tom Carson's single-block Chardonnay and Pinot Noir program, poured from a relaxed cellar door with one of the Peninsula's loveliest lunch decks

Yabby Lake sits slightly east of the main wine-country road, and that off-axis position has worked in its favour. The Kirby family planted the vineyard in 1998 and hired Tom Carson to run the winemaking  -  and what the team has built in the years since is one of the most serious single-block programs in the country. The flagship Block 1 Pinot Noir became the first Pinot ever to win the Jimmy Watson Memorial Trophy in 2014. The Block 1 Chardonnay is, quietly, one of the best Chardonnays in Australia.

The cellar door is open daily and is deliberately more relaxed than the winemaking philosophy suggests. Seated tastings on the deck, a short early-lunch menu, and room to work through a full flight at your own pace. This is the cellar door we recommend when someone wants to understand why Peninsula Chardonnay is currently among the most interesting in the country.

Order the Block 1 flight. Stay for lunch. Buy the single-vineyard Chardonnay on the way out  -  it rewards five years in the cellar.
